dubai/nad-al-sheba.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover both IGCSE boards, A Level subjects and the IB Diploma and Middle Years programmes taught in and around Nad Al Sheba. Send the week's activity schedule with your enquiry rather than only the subject, because out here the hour is harder to find than the specialist.

intro.heading: The hour you are looking for is already spoken for
paragraphs: Nad Al Sheba sits inland from the creek, between Meydan and the Dubai-Al Ain Road, with villa communities, equestrian facilities and a cluster of well-known private schools either inside it or on its edge. Unusually for Dubai, many families here have a school within a short drive, which removes the problem that dominates most of the city. It introduces a different one.

When the school run is short, families fill the recovered time. In this community that means sport, and a serious amount of it: football, swimming, riding, tennis, cricket, martial arts, often at a competitive level with fixed training evenings and weekend fixtures. Add music lessons, a drama production, a scouting group or a religious class, and a typical week has three or four evenings already committed before homework is considered.

That is not a problem to be solved by removing the activities. For many students the training is the best thing in their week and the reason they cope with the academic load. It is, though, the reason so many tutoring arrangements in this community fail. A family books the only visibly empty slot, that slot turns out to be the one evening with no commitment, and within a month the student is doing seven consecutive committed evenings with nothing left over. Then something gets cancelled, and it is rarely the training.

The second feature here is the range of academic routes within a very small area. Families in Nad Al Sheba can choose between a British route running IGCSE then A Levels, an IB continuum route running the Middle Years Programme then the Diploma, and schools offering a mix. Those routes diverge at sixteen in ways that affect coursework load, examination timing and how much independent work a student carries, and a family choosing between them is making a decision that shapes the next four years.

Third, siblings frequently end up on different routes, because schools are chosen one child at a time and places come up when they come up. A household with one child sitting A Level examinations in the summer and another managing Diploma internal assessments through the autumn is running two academic calendars in one kitchen, with different deadlines, different reporting and different kinds of pressure.

So this page is about the practical half of all that: where the free hour actually is, what the evening roads do to a late session, what each route at sixteen commits a student to, what the market charges in dirhams, and what a tutor may and may not do with assessed work on either route. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Nad Al Sheba lesson is one-to-one over live video.

dubai/nad-al-sheba.programmesIntro: Four routes are in play in this community. For each, the detail that matters here is how much independent evening work it demands of a student who is already training four nights a week.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at sixteen across eight or nine subjects in parallel. Cambridge examines in June and November series and tiers many subjects into Core and Extended; Pearson Edexcel examines in May/June and November on a 9-1 scale. The load is broad rather than deep, which means a lot of small homework tasks rather than a few large ones.
programmes.countryNote: Broad loads suit a student with committed evenings better than deep ones, because a twenty-minute task fits into a gap and a two-hour essay does not. The Year 11 pinch comes when mocks, coursework and training fixtures land in the same six weeks, which is the point most Nad Al Sheba families get in touch.

programmes.name: A Level and AS Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, with most or all of the assessment external and some subjects carrying non-examined assessment. Fewer subjects means fewer separate deadlines, but each piece of work is longer and demands sustained concentration rather than short bursts.
programmes.countryNote: For a student with four training evenings, A Levels can be the easier fit in one way and harder in another: there are fewer deadlines to track, but the work needs uninterrupted blocks. Weekend mornings become structurally important rather than optional, and that is worth planning in Year 12 rather than discovering in Year 13.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed components run through both years against school deadlines set well before any board date, so the pressure is continuous rather than concentrated in one examination season.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma's CAS requirement means a student already training competitively has a natural fit for part of the core. The continuous coursework load is the harder part, because it competes with fixtures all year rather than only in May, and it is the main reason Diploma families here book a coursework block.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four lettered criteria with task-specific descriptors rather than percentages. Assessment is continuous and task-based, and the Personal Project in the final year is self-managed and lands alongside mock examinations.
programmes.countryNote: For an active student the Middle Years Programme rewards planning: tasks are known in advance and can be worked around fixtures if somebody writes them on a calendar. The families who struggle are the ones who treat each task as a surprise, which it almost never is.

dubai/nad-al-sheba.subjectsIntro: Requests from this community lean towards the sciences and mathematics at Higher Level and A Level, with regular essay-subject work where sustained writing is the thing a packed week squeezes out.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-and-calculus Diploma route, where fluency accumulates through steady practice. A student training four evenings a week needs short daily practice rather than one long weekly session, because algebraic automaticity decays faster than content knowledge does.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and calculator fluency. Marks leak on interpretation questions that ask what a value means in context, which is a separate skill from calculating it and has to be practised deliberately.

subjects.name: A Level Mathematics and Further Mathematics
subjects.description: Depth over breadth, with pure, mechanics and statistics strands. Further Mathematics is a significant additional commitment and is worth discussing against the training calendar before it is chosen rather than after.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: HL, SL, A Level and IGCSE
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms, energetics and quantitative work decide the upper grades on every route. The internally assessed investigation rewards a narrow, well-controlled question with honest treatment of uncertainty, not the ambitious project most students first propose.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: HL, SL, A Level and IGCSE
subjects.description: Mechanics and electricity hold the marks. At the higher levels the binding skill is turning a described situation into an equation quickly enough to finish the paper, which is built by volume rather than by explanation.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: HL, SL, A Level and IGCSE
subjects.description: A vocabulary-dense subject where fluent paraphrase scores nothing against a scheme requiring specific terms. It is the most self-studiable science, which makes it a good candidate to manage independently during a heavy fixture period.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.levels: HL, SL, A Level and IGCSE
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is the fastest available gain on every route: axes, curves, labels and shifts earn marks prose cannot. The higher levels add quantitative questions and policy papers that reward precise named examples.

subjects.name: English Literature and English A
subjects.description: The subject a packed week damages most, because it needs uninterrupted reading and writing time. Essay plans against past questions are the efficient drill: fifteen minutes each, and they test the skill the examiner is marking.

subjects.name: Business Management and Business Studies
subjects.levels: HL, SL, A Level and IGCSE
subjects.description: Applying a tool to a named organisation rather than describing it. The research projects need a narrow question and real sources, and settling the question early saves weeks that a student with fixtures cannot spare later.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Compulsory in all Dubai private schools, taught in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because the expectations and the language of instruction differ. Short, frequent practice holds vocabulary better than a single weekly hour.

sections.heading: Finding the free hour by subtraction
paragraphs: The mistake almost every family in this community makes is to look for an empty slot. There is usually exactly one, and taking it means the student now has no evening at all without a commitment. That works until the first week something runs late, and then the tutoring is what moves, because the training has a coach and a team and the tutoring has neither.

The better method is subtraction. Lay out the whole week including fixtures, training, rehearsals and the hour homework genuinely takes, and then look for the hour currently producing least. In this community that is very often a weekday evening slot spent on homework that is being done inattentively between other commitments, or a Friday afternoon that produces nothing. Converting one of those into a supervised technique hour adds no time to the week at all.

Where genuinely nothing can be subtracted, the honest options are a weekend morning or deciding not to start this term. We would rather a family begin in January with a slot that holds than in October with one that collapses by half-term. An arrangement that quietly stops after four sessions has usually been scheduled into a week with no room in it, and nobody involved enjoys that outcome.

The last part of the method is status. A session that is treated as the flexible item in the week will be the item that flexes. Families who tell us the hour is fixed, and then treat it that way, get a different result from families who treat it as something to fit in. That is not a criticism of either; it is the single best predictor we have of whether an arrangement is still running in March.

sections.heading: The evening roads: Ras Al Khor, Al Khail and the Al Ain road
paragraphs: Nad Al Sheba's school run is short, but its evening roads are not quiet. The community is bounded by routes that carry commuter and inter-emirate traffic: the Dubai-Al Ain Road to the south-east, Al Khail Road to the west, and the Ras Al Khor road to the north-east. A session scheduled after an activity often depends on a drive back from a training venue rather than from school, and training venues are spread across the city.

This is the detail that distinguishes scheduling here from scheduling in a district where the only journey is the school run. A student who finishes swimming in Al Quoz at 6:30pm is not available at seven, whatever the map says, because the drive home crosses Sheikh Zayed Road at a bad hour. A student training within the community is available fifteen minutes after they finish.

The practical approach is to ask where the activity happens, not just when it finishes. We then set the session from the realistic arrival home, with a buffer, exactly as we would from a school bus. For families with venues outside the community, the answer is frequently that a post-activity weekday session does not work at all and the hour belongs on a morning.

One advantage worth using: because school journeys here are short, the window between school finishing and the first activity is often genuinely free and under-used. A session at 3:45pm, before training at 5:30pm, uses an hour that would otherwise be spent waiting, and it leaves the evening intact. Families rarely consider it because the afternoon feels like it belongs to the child, and for some students it should. For others it is the best hour available all week.

sections.heading: Sport, music and the one hour that is left
paragraphs: It is worth writing the week down honestly, because families consistently underestimate how committed it is. Four training evenings is common here. A weekend fixture takes a morning and sometimes a day. Music lessons and practice add two or three short sessions. A production, in the term it runs, can take two evenings a week for six weeks. Homework in Year 11 or at A Level is ninety minutes to two hours on a weekday.

None of those should automatically be cut. Competitive sport at this level teaches scheduling, resilience and the ability to perform under pressure, which transfer directly to examinations. A student who gives up their sport to add two tutoring hours may end up worse at both. The Diploma's CAS requirement explicitly values this kind of commitment, and for an active student that part of the core is effectively already done.

What can be cut, usually, is unproductive study time. A student doing homework with a phone beside them for two hours is doing about fifty minutes of homework. Converting that into fifty focused minutes plus a supervised technique hour costs nothing in total time and changes what the evening produces. Families are often surprised that the fix is not more hours but better ones.

The table below is a way of writing the week out. The point of it is the final column: having identified the remaining hour, decide deliberately what it is for, rather than letting whatever is most urgent that week occupy it. An hour that goes to the loudest deadline every week is the hour nobody is learning in.

sections.heading: Two routes in one house: siblings on different examinations
paragraphs: Because schools in this part of Dubai are chosen one child at a time and places arrive when they arrive, siblings in the same household frequently end up on different academic routes. One child sits A Level examinations concentrated in a summer season; another manages Diploma internal assessments spread across two years. The household is running two calendars with different shapes.

The practical consequences are mostly about attention and timing. The A Level student's pressure arrives in a block and is visible: everybody in the house knows when the examinations are. The Diploma student's pressure is continuous and invisible: a coursework deadline in November matters as much to the final grade as an examination in May, and it is much easier for a busy household to miss.

The fix is a single shared calendar with both children's assessed deadlines on it, obtained from each school rather than reconstructed from memory. Schools publish internal coursework deadlines, mock windows and examination dates; a parent who asks for them in September can see the collisions in advance and plan the tutoring and the fixtures around them.

Resource allocation is the harder conversation. Where a budget supports one subject, the honest guidance is to spend on the deadline that is closest and least recoverable rather than on the child who is complaining most. A Diploma coursework component that is submitted badly cannot be revised away in April; an A Level mock in February can be. That is not favouritism, it is sequencing, and explaining it that way to both children usually works better than pretending the spend is equal.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in this corridor, in dirhams
paragraphs: Most pages serving this market publish no price at all, and two of the ones that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. The figures below are market rates attributed to the providers that published them. They describe the market and are not an IB Gram price list.

Read from the bottom up, the published rates form a ladder rather than a single price. Generalists and university students advertise online help from roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform starting near AED 33. A qualified subject tutor online falls between about AED 150 and AED 300; one agency publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. An in-home one-to-one visit is listed at roughly AED 180 to AED 350 on one index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors, the drive billed inside the rate. At the top, specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, one agency at AED 270, and one premium provider at AED 650.

Set that against the rest of the household's commitments. Competitive sports academy fees, music tuition and equipment in a community like this frequently exceed what a weekly academic hour costs, which is worth knowing when a family describes tutoring as the expensive item. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not increase for the 2026-27 academic year, so the fee line is at least stable while other costs are not.

Monthly figures circulating in this market include about AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. One published index estimates weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. We quote only after seeing a marked script and the week's commitments.

sections.heading: A tutor driving to Nad Al Sheba against one-to-one online
paragraphs: An in-home tutor is a genuine option in this market and a villa here has the room for it, which removes the objection that applies in apartment districts. An adult at the table sees written working without being asked and can annotate a page directly, and younger children often respond better to a person than a screen.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. In this community the decisive factor is not cost or even tutor pool; it is the schedule. A household whose week is built around fixed training times needs a session that can move to a morning when a fixture is rearranged, start fifteen minutes after a student walks in from a local training session, or be taken from a hotel during a tournament weekend. An in-home arrangement cannot do any of those.

There is a second scheduling argument. Tutoring in this community is often concentrated into pinch windows, four to six weeks when mocks, coursework and a competitive season collide. A short intensive block with a specialist is easy to arrange online and difficult to arrange in person, because the person who can teach Higher Level chemistry for six weeks in February is not necessarily willing to drive to Nad Al Sheba twice a week in February.

What online gives up: unprompted sight of the page, which we replace with a phone or tablet camera over the working and a tutor who insists on seeing method rather than hearing answers; and the presence of an adult in the room, which matters more for younger students.

sections.heading: Choosing between A Levels and the IB Diploma at sixteen
paragraphs: Both routes are available within a few minutes of each other here, and the choice is usually made on school reputation rather than on which structure suits the student. That is understandable and it is the wrong order. The two routes make genuinely different demands, and for a student with heavy commitments outside school the structural differences matter more than the branding.

A Levels concentrate. Three or four subjects studied deeply, assessment largely external, fewer separate deadlines to track, and a single examination season that dominates the final spring. The risk is narrowness: a subject dropped at sixteen is difficult to pick up, and a student uncertain of direction closes doors earlier.

The Diploma spreads. Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, with internally assessed components running across two years on school-set deadlines. Breadth is retained and nothing closes early, but the student is managing continuous assessment rather than preparing for one season, and that demands organisation more than brilliance.

For tutoring, the implication is practical. An A Level student typically needs fewer subjects supported but longer, uninterrupted sessions, which pushes towards weekend mornings. A Diploma student typically needs shorter, more frequent contact spread across the year, with concentrated blocks around coursework deadlines. Neither is cheaper overall, but they are differently shaped, and a family that plans the shape in Year 11 avoids discovering it in Year 13. Whichever route is chosen, check the published entry requirements of the specific university programmes your child may apply to, because those are set by the institution and change.

sections.heading: The honesty line on both routes
paragraphs: Each route has assessed work that must be the student's own, and the rules are strict on both. On the Diploma that means internal assessments in every subject, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge. On the A Level route it means non-examined assessment in the subjects that carry it. Both carry declarations, and both carry malpractice consequences for the candidate rather than for anyone who helped.

One provider found in this search sells completed Internal Assessments outright. The transaction looks like a shortcut and is an integrity breach that the student signs for. In a community where students are used to coaching in other parts of their lives, the distinction between coaching and substitution is worth drawing explicitly, because a swimming coach can correct your stroke in the water and an academic tutor cannot write your sentence.

The boundary: a tutor may teach the content the assessment rests on, explain each criterion and what its marks reward, say whether a research question is viable before weeks are spent on it, warn that a method will not generate usable data, read a draft and name the criterion that is under-served, and ask the questions that make a student see their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, pick the question, or edit a draft into a finished state.

We also do not redistribute board material. Syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. We reference them, name the official source and work from what the school has issued. The test any student can apply alone: if the help would still work with you out of the room, it is substitution.

sections.heading: Starting when the term is already running
paragraphs: Most enquiries from this community arrive mid-term, after a report or a mock, into a week that was fully allocated in September. Adding an hour at that point is a real decision rather than an administrative one, and it works best when it is treated that way.

Three things before the first session: a recent marked script or report, the board and syllabus code with the tier where one applies, and the week as it actually is, including fixtures and training. The third is the one families leave out and the one that determines whether the arrangement survives.

The first session is a diagnostic. The tutor works through the script with your child, has them re-attempt a question live, and writes a short note naming the gap, the order to address it and a realistic timescale. Sometimes that note says the problem is not the subject but the fact that two hours of homework are being done in four hours with a phone present, in which case the recommendation is about the week rather than about tutoring.

On availability: weekday slots between 4:00pm and 6:00pm are contested across the whole of Dubai, and in this community the ones before activities start are contested within it as well. For scarce Higher Level and A Level subjects we may need more than a week to match the right person, and we will say so at the enquiry rather than taking a booking and finding somebody approximate. No competitor page in this market publishes a coverage limit; we publish ours.

faqs.question: How do we fit tutoring around four training evenings a week in Nad Al Sheba?
faqs.answer: Not by taking the one empty evening, which is usually your child's only uncommitted one. Lay out the whole term including fixtures, training, music and the hour homework genuinely takes, then look for the hour currently producing least. In this community that is very often homework being done inattentively alongside a phone, or a Friday afternoon that produces nothing. Converting one of those adds no time to the week. If genuinely nothing can be subtracted, take a weekend morning or wait for next term.

faqs.question: Should my child give up competitive sport to make room for tutoring?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and we will say so. Competitive training teaches scheduling, resilience and performing under pressure, all of which transfer directly to examinations, and for the IB Diploma the CAS requirement explicitly values that kind of commitment. A student who drops their sport to add two academic hours often ends up worse at both. The hour worth reclaiming is the unfocused study time, not the one thing in the week your child is looking forward to.

faqs.question: Can a session start right after training finishes?
faqs.answer: It depends where the training is. A student finishing at a venue inside Nad Al Sheba can start fifteen minutes after they walk in. A student finishing in Al Quoz or out along the Dubai-Al Ain Road is crossing commuter traffic at the evening peak, and a post-activity weekday session usually does not work at all for them. We ask where the activity happens, not only when it ends, and for the second group the honest answer is a weekend or an early-afternoon slot.

faqs.question: Is the 3:45pm slot before activities any good?
faqs.answer: In this community it is frequently the best hour available all week, and it is the one families consider last. Because school journeys here are short, the window between the school finish and the first training session is often spent waiting. A session in it leaves the evening intact and meets a student who is not yet tired. The trade-off is that the afternoon feels like the child's own time, and for some students it should be. For others it is the slot that saves the plan.

faqs.question: We have one child on A Levels and one on the IB Diploma. How do we manage both?
faqs.answer: With one shared calendar carrying both children's assessed deadlines, obtained from each school in September rather than reconstructed later. The A Level student's pressure arrives in a visible block; the Diploma student's is continuous and much easier for a busy household to miss, even though a November coursework component counts as much as a May paper. Where a budget covers one subject, spend on the deadline that is closest and least recoverable rather than on the child complaining loudest.

faqs.question: Which is better for an active student, A Levels or the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: They are differently shaped rather than better or worse. A Levels concentrate: three or four subjects, largely external assessment, few deadlines and one dominant examination season, which suits a student who can protect long uninterrupted blocks, usually at weekends. The Diploma spreads: six subjects, internal assessment in each, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, which demands organisation across two years. Decide which structure your child can actually run, then check the published entry requirements of the universities they may apply to.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to villas in Nad Al Sheba?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. Here the decisive factor is the schedule rather than the cost: a household built around fixed training times needs a session that can move to a morning when a fixture is rearranged, start soon after local training ends, or run from a hotel during a tournament weekend. An in-home arrangement cannot do any of those.

faqs.question: What happens to lessons during a tournament or a competition week?
faqs.answer: They move rather than disappear. A session can shift to a morning, to another evening in the same week, or run from wherever your child is staying if there is a desk and a connection. For a known competition block we would usually plan around it in advance: lighter contact during the week itself, and a catch-up session afterwards that begins by marking whatever independent work was set. What we try to avoid is cancelling, because two cancellations in three weeks is how an arrangement ends.

faqs.question: How much does A Level tutoring cost compared with IGCSE in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published market figures group A Level with IB and IGCSE specialists at roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour and above, with one agency quoting AED 270 and a premium provider AED 650, against IGCSE from about AED 150 at one agency. The gap reflects the smaller pool of tutors who can teach a subject in the depth A Level requires, not a premium on the label. Those are other providers' published rates in dirhams, not ours; we quote after seeing a marked script.

faqs.question: What is a pinch window and how do we plan for it?
faqs.answer: It is the four to six weeks where mock examinations, coursework deadlines and a competitive season collide, and almost every household here has one. Identify it in September from the school's published dates and the fixture list, then plan a short intensive block with a defined objective and an end point rather than reacting in the week it starts. Sessions in a pinch window can be short and frequent, because the student needs feedback faster than usual, and the block stops when the window closes.

faqs.question: My child does two hours of homework and seems to achieve very little. Why?
faqs.answer: Because two hours of homework with a phone present is usually about fifty minutes of homework spread across two hours. The study is interrupted often enough that nothing sustained happens, and the student ends up tired without having produced much. The fix is structural rather than academic: a defined block, the phone in another room, and a clear finishing point. Families who do that frequently find the spare hour they were looking for, without adding anything to the week.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an Extended Essay for a student with a heavy fixture calendar?
faqs.answer: Within the boundary, and the Extended Essay is the component a fixture-heavy year damages most, because it needs sustained independent work between school supervisor meetings. A tutor can explain the criteria, say whether the research question is viable, warn where the method will not produce usable material and read a draft to name the weak criterion. A tutor cannot supply text, rewrite sections or edit a draft into a finished state. Agree what gets done before a competition block, not afterwards.

faqs.question: How is academic coaching different from the coaching my child already gets?
faqs.answer: The boundary sits in a different place and it is worth saying out loud, because students used to sports coaching sometimes misread it. A swimming coach can hold a position, correct a stroke in the water and intervene physically in the performance. An academic tutor working on assessed coursework cannot write a sentence, rewrite a section or produce data, because the work carries a declaration that it is the student's own. Everything legitimate requires the student to be the one doing the thinking.

faqs.question: How quickly can you arrange a first session for a Nad Al Sheba family?
faqs.answer: For mainstream IGCSE and Standard Level subjects, usually within a few days once we have the marked script, the syllabus code and the week's real commitments. Scarce Higher Level and A Level subjects take longer, sometimes over a week, because the pool of tutors who can teach them to that depth is small and the contested 4:00pm to 6:00pm window fills. We say that at the enquiry rather than accepting a booking and finding somebody approximate, which no other page in this market does.

dubai/nad-al-sheba.closingHeading: Protect one hour, and use it properly
dubai/nad-al-sheba.closingBody: Nad Al Sheba families rarely need more tutoring hours. They need one hour that genuinely holds, in a week that was fully allocated in September. Write the week out honestly, fixtures and all. Find the hour currently producing least, which is usually two hours of homework being done in four with a phone nearby. Give the session the same status as a training commitment, use weekend mornings for the work that needs an uninterrupted stretch, and plan the pinch window before it arrives rather than during it. Then send a marked script and the syllabus code, and the first session will be a diagnostic. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video.

dubai/oud-metha.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover both IGCSE boards, the IB Diploma and the Indian-curriculum stages taught in this district. Before matching, tell us what support your child already receives at school, because the useful question in Oud Metha is not what a tutor can teach but what the school is not able to reach.

intro.heading: Living inside the school belt changes what tutoring is for
paragraphs: Oud Metha is the one part of Dubai where a secondary-age child can realistically walk or take a five-minute drive to school. Several of the emirate's oldest private schools sit here, serving British, Indian and Catholic-foundation traditions, with cohorts large enough that a single year group can run to several hundred students. Families live among the schools rather than commuting to them, which produces two conditions that exist almost nowhere else in the city.

The first is time. A child home by 2:45pm or 3:00pm has an afternoon, not a remnant of one. A 3:30pm session is genuinely available here, which matters more than it sounds: it means homework can still be finished before the evening, and it means a session is not competing with fatigue. In Dubai Marina or Al Khawaneej that slot does not exist, and any page that promises it is describing a different neighbourhood.

The second is information. Parents here are physically closer to the school and, in the long-established institutions, often part of a community that has used it for a generation. They hear about the teacher before the report arrives. They know which subject sets a heavy written load and which year group sits frequent class tests. They also know, usually, what free support the school already runs: subject clinics, revision sessions before mocks, coursework check-ins with the teacher, departmental catch-up hours.

That second condition should change the tutoring decision and frequently does not. The commonest avoidable spend in this district is paying privately for something the school provides, badly timed against something the school cannot provide at all. A school revision clinic for twenty students covers content and cannot diagnose one child's specific habit of answering around a command term. A departmental catch-up hour covers last week's topic and cannot rebuild two years of algebraic fluency. Knowing which is which is worth more than an extra hour a week.

There is a third condition specific to this belt, and it is the size of the year groups. A Year 11 cohort of several hundred students means a subject teacher marking a very large number of mock scripts in a single week. They can tell a class precisely what the cohort got wrong, and that briefing is genuinely useful. What they cannot do is sit beside one student and watch the mistake happen in real time, which is the only way some habits get caught. Scale gives this district strong teaching and weak individual diagnosis, and knowing that is the start of spending well.

So this page is organised around the division of labour. What the school is good at, what it structurally cannot reach, where marks are lost in enough detail to act on, what the market charges in dirhams, and what a tutor may and may not do with internally assessed work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Oud Metha lesson is one-to-one over live video, which is also what makes the early slot practical, since no tutor has to cross the city to reach it.

dubai/oud-metha.programmesIntro: Three systems dominate Oud Metha, and the useful detail for each is where a large, well-resourced school still leaves a gap that only individual attention closes.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at sixteen, Cambridge in June and November series with Core and Extended tiering on many codes, Pearson Edexcel in May/June and November on a 9-1 scale. The difference that matters for tutoring is that the content is usually taught adequately in a large school and the technique is not, because technique needs one examiner-eye on one script.
programmes.countryNote: Oud Metha's secondary schools run big Year 11 cohorts. A subject teacher marking a hundred and fifty mock scripts can tell a class what went wrong; they cannot sit with each student and watch them answer. That is the specific gap private tutoring fills well here, and it is a narrower and cheaper job than full re-teaching.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed components are marked against published criteria and moderated, and the school sets internal deadlines ahead of anything the board publishes. The Extended Essay has a named school supervisor whose role is defined by the IB.
programmes.countryNote: Most Oud Metha Diploma students travel out of the district, since the nearest IB continuum schools sit across Al Garhoud Bridge or along the creek. That lengthens the afternoon and is the one case where the district's early-slot advantage disappears, so Diploma sessions here are usually placed from 4:15pm.

programmes.name: Indian-curriculum stages and the move to international boards
programmes.description: Board examinations at Grade 10 and Grade 12 with a pattern of unit tests between them, and a full-syllabus final paper that rewards breadth and retrieval. Students moving from this route into IGCSE or the Diploma meet marking conventions, not new content, and the adjustment is measured in weeks per subject.
programmes.countryNote: The district contains both the schools students leave and the schools they arrive at, so the transition work is unusually common here. It is also unusually well-informed: parents in this community generally know somebody whose child made the same move, which makes the conversation about timescales more realistic than it is elsewhere.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four lettered criteria with task-specific descriptors instead of percentages. Students joining from a percentage-based system frequently score well on knowledge and poorly on the criteria that ask for evaluation, because they have never been asked to write in that register.
programmes.countryNote: For Oud Metha families this programme usually means a change of school as well as a change of system. The practical preparation is not content but the language of the criteria, which can be taught explicitly in a short block before the move rather than discovered over two reporting cycles afterwards.

dubai/oud-metha.subjectsIntro: In a district with large science and mathematics cohorts, the subjects families bring to us are the ones where a class of thirty cannot give one student the individual marking attention that changes a grade.

subjects.name: Mathematics 0580 and 4MA1
subjects.levels: Cambridge IGCSE Extended and Pearson Edexcel
subjects.description: The volume subject. In a large class the teacher marks final answers; a tutor watches the student produce the answer and corrects the habit of omitting steps. Method marks exist for written reasoning, and recovering them is often a grade without any new content.

subjects.name: Physics 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Electricity, circuits and the practical paper. The practical questions reward a method described precisely enough for a stranger to repeat it, which is a writing standard rather than a science standard and is rarely drilled individually in a big cohort.

subjects.name: Chemistry 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and the quantitative questions that separate the top grades. Students in strong classes often follow the explanation and cannot start the calculation alone, which only shows up when somebody watches them try.

subjects.name: Biology 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Mark-scheme vocabulary is the whole game. A fluent paraphrase scores nothing where a specific term is required, and a student can read confidently while losing a third of the available marks to that single habit.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-and-calculus Diploma route. Higher Level assumes algebraic automaticity, and students who arrived at it without Additional Mathematics often need a short foundational block before the course content becomes workable.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and calculator fluency. The marks leak on interpretation: a question asking what a gradient means in context is answered with the gradient, which is arithmetic rather than interpretation.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy first. Correctly labelled axes, curves and shifts earn marks prose cannot replace. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and a policy paper where a precise real example outscores a general observation every time.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study subjects where students describe a tool instead of applying it to the organisation in the question. The Diploma research project requires a narrow question and real source material, and settling the question properly saves weeks later.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Two external papers and oral assessment, with the individual oral connecting a global issue to two texts, one in translation. Preparation beats improvisation, and structure and evidence selection carry more marks than style.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required in every Dubai private school, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. KHDA also requires that teachers of these subjects hold the authority's approval to teach them.

dubai/oud-metha.regionsTitle: Oud Metha and the districts that use its schools
dubai/oud-metha.regionsIntro: Oud Metha's schools serve a wide catchment, and the practical advice shifts with the length of the journey. These are the areas we work with around the belt.

regions.name: Karama
regions.note: A short drive or a long walk from the schools. Arrival is early, so the district's 3:30pm advantage applies, but study space in the apartment blocks usually caps the session at forty-five minutes.

regions.name: Al Mankhool
regions.note: Mid-rise apartments immediately west with the same early arrivals. Newer blocks have more usable study space, which makes a single sixty-minute weekday session realistic rather than optimistic.

regions.name: Al Jafiliya
regions.note: Close to the Trade Centre corridor and the Green Line. Working parents commute into Downtown, so sessions are often timed to overlap with a parent returning rather than with the school bell.

regions.name: Bur Dubai
regions.note: The older sub-districts north of the belt. Mixed curricula within single buildings, and journeys short enough that an early slot survives even on a busy afternoon.

regions.name: Al Nasr and Za'abeel
regions.note: Between the schools and the Trade Centre, with a mix of staff housing and apartments. Short school runs and relatively quiet afternoons make this one of the easier catchments to schedule.

regions.name: Deira
regions.note: Across the creek through Al Shindagha Tunnel or over Al Maktoum Bridge. The crossing costs fifteen to thirty minutes at school closing, which moves the first honest slot to about 4:00pm.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: East of the creek near the airport. Families here often attend schools on their own side, but those who travel into Oud Metha face the bridge approach and should plan for a later start.

regions.name: Al Satwa
regions.note: Low-rise and densely occupied towards the Jumeirah road. Street noise in the late afternoon is a genuine factor, and a headset improves a session more than extra bandwidth does.

schoolClusters.city: The Oud Metha belt itself
schoolClusters.note: Several of Dubai's longest-established private schools, within a few minutes of each other, running British, Indian and Catholic-foundation traditions with large year groups. The proximity is what gives this district its early-afternoon advantage and its unusually well-informed parent community. Students we support attend schools across this belt.
schools: The Indian High School, Oud Metha

schoolClusters.city: The nearest IB continuum options
schoolClusters.note: Oud Metha has no IB continuum school inside it, so Diploma and Middle Years students travel across the creek or along it. That journey is the one thing that removes this district's scheduling advantage, and it is why Diploma sessions here start later than IGCSE ones.

dubai/oud-metha.modesIntro: Because this district has a genuine early slot and well-resourced schools, the formats that work best are narrow and short rather than open-ended.

modes.title: Early weekday technique slot
modes.description: A sixty-minute session starting between 3:30pm and 4:00pm, used for marking, command-term work and timed questions rather than re-teaching. It exists because this is one of the few Dubai districts where a child is home, fed and settled early enough for the hour to be useful.

Homework still finished before the evening

modes.title: Short diagnostic block
modes.description: Four to six sessions with a defined question: why is this grade where it is, and what specifically moves it. The block ends with a written answer rather than a renewal. Families here often use it to decide whether the school's own support is sufficient.

modes.title: Coursework review sessions
modes.description: Spaced sessions through a coursework term, with the student working between them and the tutor reviewing against the published criteria. The school supervisor owns the formal process; a tutor adds criterion-level feedback the supervisor does not have the hours to give in detail.
bullets: Spaced to leave working time between sessions

sections.heading: What the school already provides, and where paid help is redundant
paragraphs: Large, long-established schools run a lot of free support, and in Oud Metha they run more of it than most. Subject clinics at lunchtime. Departmental revision in the weeks before mocks. Teacher check-ins on coursework. Holiday catch-up sessions in the subjects with the weakest cohort results. Any family about to pay for tutoring should find out exactly what of that is available before spending anything, because the overlap is often complete.

Where school support is strong is content and coverage. A teacher running a revision clinic knows the syllabus, knows which topics the cohort got wrong in the mock, and can re-teach them efficiently to a group. If your child's problem is that they missed three weeks with an illness, or never understood electrolysis, the school clinic is the correct answer and it is free.

Where school support structurally cannot reach is the individual habit. A teacher with a hundred and fifty Year 11 scripts can tell the class that six-mark answers need six points. They cannot sit beside your child, watch them write a six-mark answer, stop them at the third point and make them notice the pattern. That observation loop is what one-to-one buys, and it is a narrower and cheaper purchase than full re-teaching.

The second thing school support cannot reach is a structural gap from an earlier year. A revision clinic assumes the foundations are present. A student whose algebra was never automatic will sit through the clinic, follow every line, and fail to reproduce any of it, because the problem is two years upstream of the topic being revised. Diagnosing that is the first job of a decent first session, and it is the reason we ask for a marked script rather than a subject name.

sections.heading: The early slot: Oud Metha's one genuine scheduling advantage
paragraphs: Across most of Dubai, the first honest tutoring slot on a weekday is 4:15pm or later, because the school run eats the afternoon. In Oud Metha it is often 3:30pm, and that difference compounds. A session that finishes at 4:30pm leaves an evening for homework, reading and sleep. A session that finishes at 6:30pm pushes homework past eight and reading past nine, and by Thursday the student is running on a deficit that no tutor can teach around.

The advantage is not automatic. It depends on the child being physically home and settled, which for walkers and short drives means around three o'clock. It also depends on the session being the right kind of work. An early slot immediately after school is better used for marking, timed questions and technique than for new content, because a student arriving straight from six lessons has limited appetite for a seventh.

There is a trade-off worth naming. An early slot competes with after-school activities, which in this district are often held at the school itself and are a real part of a child's week. We would rather move a session to a weekend morning than displace the one thing a student looks forward to, and families who try to keep both usually end up cancelling the tutoring rather than the football.

The table below sets out what each start time suits. It is a planning aid rather than a rule, and the right answer for a specific child depends on whether they fade at four or at eight, which the first two sessions will reveal more reliably than any questionnaire.

table.caption: START TIMES AND WHAT EACH ONE IS ACTUALLY GOOD FOR
rows: Competes with school activities and clubs
Short school run, student who fades late
A full teaching hour with a settled student
Little slack if the session overruns
Students who concentrate better after dinner
A full timed paper plus marking

sections.heading: Describe, explain, calculate: what the command verb is worth
paragraphs: The single most transferable thing a tutor can teach an IGCSE or Diploma student is to read the verb. Every question begins with an instruction that tells the student what kind of answer earns marks, and most students answer with whatever they know about the topic instead. A six-mark question beginning "evaluate" and answered with six facts scores a fraction of the available marks, and the student walks out believing they knew the material, which they did.

This is also the cheapest grade available, because it requires no new content. A student who already knows the topic and learns to answer inside the verb can move a grade in a term. The work is dull and repetitive: take a past paper, cover the answers, identify the verb in each question, say what the examiner is asking for, then write the answer and check it against the scheme. Twenty questions of that is worth more than two hours of re-explanation.

The verbs differ between boards and between subjects, and the published assessment materials define them. That is one reason practising on the wrong code costs marks: a term used in a Cambridge syllabus may carry a slightly different expectation in a Pearson specification, and a student who has internalised the wrong version answers confidently and incorrectly.

The table lists the verbs that account for most of the loss we see in marked scripts from this district. It is not a complete list and it is not a substitute for the board's own published definitions, which the school can provide and which should be the reference point for any serious revision.

table.caption: COMMAND VERBS AND THE ANSWER THAT ACTUALLY SCORES
rows: A paragraph that buries the fact
What happens, in sequence, without reasons
Explaining why, which is a different verb
Reasons linked in a causal chain
Working shown, units given, answer stated
A correct answer with no visible method
Explicit points of similarity and difference
Two separate descriptions side by side
Both sides weighed, then a judgement
One side argued well, no judgement

sections.heading: Three places an IGCSE science mark disappears
paragraphs: Science marks in this district rarely disappear because a student does not know the science. They disappear in three specific places, and once a parent can name them the school report becomes readable rather than mysterious.

The first is the extended-response question. A six-mark question needs six separate creditable points, and a student who writes three of them very well scores three. The habit comes from essay subjects, where quality of expression earns credit, and it has to be deliberately unlearned. The fix is counting: write the answer, count the distinct points, compare to the marks available.

The second is the practical or method question. A description of an experiment has to be precise enough for a stranger to repeat it, which means naming the measured variable, the controlled variables, the instrument and the repeats. Students describe what they did in the lesson, which is a memory rather than a method, and the mark scheme credits the method. This is a writing problem presented as a science problem, and it responds quickly to being named.

The third is the calculation under time pressure. A student who can do the mole calculation in a quiet room cannot always do it on paper four of a timed paper with six minutes left. That is not a knowledge gap, it is automaticity, and it is built by volume under the clock rather than by further explanation. A tutor whose answer to this is more teaching has misdiagnosed it.
bullets: Six-mark answers need six points, not three good ones
Method questions credit precision, not recollection
Calculations fail on automaticity, not understanding
Each of the three responds to a different kind of practice

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Oud Metha, with the figures attributed
paragraphs: Pricing in this market is unusually opaque. Three of the most visible competitor pages publish no figure at all, and two of those that do quote in US dollars rather than dirhams. Everything below is a market rate published by the provider named, presented as the market and not as an IB Gram price list. The reason a page in this district should publish them is that Oud Metha parents compare notes, and an informed comparison is better for everyone than a rumour.

Budget online tutoring from university students and generalists is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform quoting from about AED 33. Qualified subject tutors working online sit between about AED 150 and AED 300, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home visits carry travel inside the rate at roughly AED 180 to AED 350 from one published cost index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with one agency at AED 270 and one premium provider at AED 650.

Monthly figures in circulation include about AED 799 for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. One published index estimates weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year work.

In a district where the school already provides free content support, the rational spend is narrow and short: a diagnostic block at the mid or specialist band, aimed at the specific habit the school cannot reach, rather than a standing weekly hour at the budget band aimed at the same material the lunchtime clinic covers. That is a smaller total outlay than most families expect and it is the recommendation we make most often here.

sections.heading: When the drive is short, is an in-home tutor the better buy?
paragraphs: This is the one Dubai district where the usual argument against in-home tutoring weakens. The travel is short, the schools are close, and a tutor living in or near Bur Dubai can reach an Oud Metha address without an hour on Sheikh Zayed Road. Families here reasonably ask why they would choose a screen when a person could be at the table in ten minutes, and the answer is not the one most online providers give.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. The honest reason is not that in-home teaching is inferior. It is that the specific thing we are selling, a tutor matched precisely to a board, a code and a level, cannot be delivered by a local pool. The number of people who can give criterion-level feedback on a Diploma chemistry investigation is small, and almost none of them live in Bur Dubai.

There is a second argument that applies specifically where the school is strong. If the school already covers content well, the remaining job is narrow: marking, technique, a particular habit. That job does not benefit much from physical presence, and it benefits considerably from being done by someone who has marked that paper many times. Trading precision of match for proximity is a worse deal here than almost anywhere, because the content-teaching role, where presence helps most, is largely already filled.

What in-home still wins: a younger child who responds better to a person than a screen, immediate sight of written work without a camera, and independence from a connection. Those are real and we will say so rather than pretending the comparison is one-sided.

sections.heading: The Extended Essay and the Internal Assessment: who owns what
paragraphs: Confusion about roles causes most of the coursework trouble we see, and it is easily cleared up. The Extended Essay has a school-appointed supervisor whose responsibilities are defined by the IB, including a set number of recorded meetings and an authenticity declaration. Internal Assessments are set, supported and marked by the subject teacher, against published criteria, and moderated externally. Those roles belong to the school and cannot be transferred to a private tutor.

What a private tutor can legitimately add is depth of criterion feedback that a teacher supervising many students does not have hours for. Reading a draft and saying which criterion is under-served, and why, takes time proportional to the draft. A teacher with twenty supervisees cannot give each of them two hours of that; a tutor working with one student can.

The boundary is firm. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain each criterion and its marks, say whether a research question is viable before weeks are lost on it, warn that a method will not produce usable data, read a draft and name the weak criterion, and ask the questions that make a student see their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, pick the question, or edit a draft into a finished state. The student declares the work as their own and must be able to discuss it.

One provider in this market sells completed Internal Assessments. For an Oud Metha family that is worth knowing about specifically, because these schools have large Diploma cohorts and the offer circulates among students. The consequence under board malpractice rules falls on the candidate, and no refund exists for a withdrawn diploma.

A tutor adds criterion-level depth the school cannot resource

sections.heading: Joining mid-term without breaking a week that already works
paragraphs: Most enquiries from this district arrive mid-term, after a report or a mock result, into a week that is already full: school, mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education lessons, an activity or two, homework, and in many households a religious or community commitment. Adding an hour is not free, and adding it badly produces a child who is tired in every one of those slots rather than better at one.

The sequence we use is to subtract before adding. Look at the week, find the hour that is currently producing least, and put the session there. Very often that is a second evening of unsupervised homework that is being done inattentively anyway. Converting that into a supervised technique hour costs the student nothing in time and changes what the hour produces.

Where nothing can be subtracted, the honest options are a weekend morning or waiting until the next term. We would rather a family start in January with a slot that holds than start in November with one that collapses by the third week. Tutoring that stops after four sessions has usually been scheduled into a week with no room in it.

Finally, the end point. We agree in advance what the block is for and when it finishes, and the review uses the school's own next assessment rather than an impression. In a district where parents talk to each other and to teachers, an arrangement that cannot explain its own results is quickly and correctly abandoned.
bullets: Subtract an unproductive hour before adding a new one
A second evening of inattentive homework is the usual candidate
A weekend morning beats a weekday hour that will collapse
Agree the end point and review against school data

process.title: List what the school already provides
process.description: Clinics, pre-mock revision, coursework check-ins, holiday catch-up. We ask for this first because the commonest avoidable spend in this district is buying privately what the school runs free, while the gap it cannot reach stays unaddressed.

process.title: Send one marked script
process.description: A recent marked paper shows whether the loss is content, command terms, method precision or timing. Those four need different interventions, and a description of the problem cannot distinguish between them the way a script can.

process.title: Take a short diagnostic block
process.description: Four to six sessions with one question to answer: what specifically moves this grade. It ends with a written recommendation rather than an automatic renewal, and sometimes the recommendation is that the school's own support is enough.

process.title: Place the slot by subtraction
process.description: We find the hour in the week producing least, usually a second evening of unsupervised homework, and use that rather than adding to a full schedule. An early 3:30pm slot is genuinely available here where the school run is short.

process.title: Review against the next school assessment
process.description: The baseline is the marked script we started from; the test is whatever the school sets next. The tutor explains the outcome either way, and the four honest results are continue, change format, change subject, or stop.

whyPoints.title: We ask what the school gives you first
whyPoints.description: In a district with well-resourced, long-established schools, the right private purchase is narrow. We start by identifying what free support already exists so the paid hour goes to the gap it cannot reach, rather than duplicating a lunchtime clinic.

whyPoints.title: The early slot is real here
whyPoints.description: Oud Metha is one of the few Dubai areas where a 3:30pm weekday session genuinely works, because children are home and settled by three. That protects the evening for homework and sleep, which no amount of tutoring can substitute for.

whyPoints.title: Technique rather than re-teaching
whyPoints.description: Command verbs, method precision, point-counting on extended responses and timed automaticity. These are the losses a large class cannot address individually, and they are usually a grade without a single piece of new content.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the code, not the subject
whyPoints.description: Cambridge and Pearson define their command terms and structure their papers differently. We confirm the specification before matching, because confident practice on the wrong code produces confident wrong answers.

whyPoints.title: Rates published and attributed
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here belongs to the provider that published it, in the currency Dubai families use. We do not quote before seeing the problem and we will recommend the cheaper option when it is the right one.

whyPoints.title: Clear about who owns the coursework
whyPoints.description: The Extended Essay supervisor and the subject teacher hold roles defined by the IB and the school. A tutor adds criterion depth and nothing else: no text supplied, no draft finished, no data produced.

faqs.question: My child's school in Oud Metha already runs revision clinics. Do we still need a tutor?
faqs.answer: Often not, and that is worth establishing before spending anything. School clinics are good at content: re-teaching a topic the class got wrong, covering material missed through absence. They cannot sit with one student, watch them answer a six-mark question and correct the habit that is costing half the marks. If your child understands the material and the grade is still stuck, that individual observation is what paid tutoring buys. If they simply missed three weeks of lessons, the clinic is the right answer and it is free.

faqs.question: Can a tutoring session really start at 3:30pm in Oud Metha?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of very few Dubai districts where it genuinely works. Children attending schools in the belt are frequently home by 2:45pm or 3:00pm, so a 3:30pm start meets a student who is settled rather than exhausted. The session should be marking and technique rather than new content, because nobody wants a seventh lesson immediately after six. The trade-off is that the slot competes with school activities, and we would move to a weekend morning before displacing those.

faqs.question: What is the fastest way to raise an IGCSE science grade without new content?
faqs.answer: Teach the student to count. A six-mark extended-response question requires six separate creditable points, and students who write three excellent ones score three. The drill is mechanical: write the answer, count the distinct points, compare with the marks available, then check against the mark scheme. The second fastest is method precision on practical questions, where the scheme credits a description a stranger could repeat rather than a recollection of the lesson. Both are habits, both are quick, and neither requires reteaching.

faqs.question: Which command words cost students the most marks?
faqs.answer: Explain, evaluate and calculate, in that order from what we see in marked scripts. Explain requires a causal chain and is answered with description. Evaluate requires both sides weighed and then a judgement, and is answered with one side argued well and no judgement at all. Calculate requires visible working and units, and is answered with a correct final number and nothing else, which forfeits the method marks. The board's published assessment materials define these terms and the school can supply them.

faqs.question: Do you tutor at home in Oud Metha, given the schools are so close?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Travel really is short here, so the usual argument weakens, but the reason stands: we match on board, syllabus code and level, and the people who can give criterion-level feedback on a Diploma chemistry investigation are few and almost none of them live nearby. Where the school already covers content, trading match precision for proximity is a poor exchange.

faqs.question: How much does a short diagnostic block of tutoring cost in this market?
faqs.answer: Four to six sessions at the mid or specialist band. Published market figures put qualified subject tutors online at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and specialist IB or A Level tutors at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. A six-session block therefore sits in the low four figures in dirhams at the mid band. Those are other providers' published rates, not ours, and we quote only after seeing a marked script.

faqs.question: Who supervises the Extended Essay, and can a tutor take that role?
faqs.answer: No. The Extended Essay supervisor is appointed by the school and the role is defined by the IB, including recorded meetings and an authenticity declaration. The same applies to Internal Assessments, which the subject teacher supports and marks against published criteria before external moderation. A private tutor can add depth of criterion feedback that a teacher supervising twenty students cannot resource, but cannot assume the supervisor's role, supply text, or edit a draft into a finished state.

faqs.question: My child understands the work but runs out of time in exams. What fixes that?
faqs.answer: Volume under the clock, not more explanation. Running out of time is an automaticity problem: the student can perform each step, but not quickly enough to finish while also thinking. The remedy is repeated timed practice on the correct board's papers, with marking afterwards, until the routine steps stop requiring thought. A tutor whose response to a timing problem is further teaching has misdiagnosed it, and you will have paid for a term of the wrong intervention.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for tutoring in Year 10, or should we wait for Year 11?
faqs.answer: Year 10 is usually the better investment on Cambridge subjects, because that is when the Core or Extended tier decision is made and the tier caps the grade available in Year 11. It is also when habits form: the student who learns to show method and read command verbs at fourteen carries that through both years. Year 11 tutoring is often remedial and competes with mocks, coursework and the entry deadlines. Starting earlier buys a cheaper intervention.

faqs.question: How do we avoid paying for something the school is already doing?
faqs.answer: Make a list before you enquire anywhere. Write down what support the school runs and when: lunchtime clinics, pre-mock revision, coursework check-ins, holiday catch-up, past-paper packs. Then ask the tutor what they would do that is not on that list. A good answer is specific and narrow: mark your child's script with them, correct a named habit, drill timed questions. A vague answer about building confidence usually means duplication at a specialist rate.

faqs.question: Does KHDA inspect the schools in this belt, and does the rating matter for tutoring?
faqs.answer: KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai and inspects schools on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. The rating describes the school as a whole, not your child's year group or subject, and a strong overall band can still sit alongside a weak department. For tutoring purposes the useful document is your child's own marked script, not the inspection report, though the report is worth reading for what it says about specific subject outcomes.

faqs.question: Can tutoring start mid-term without overloading an already full week?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you subtract before adding. Look for the hour producing least, which is very often a second evening of unsupervised homework being done inattentively. Converting that into a supervised technique hour costs no extra time and changes what the hour produces. Where nothing can be subtracted, a weekend morning or waiting for the next term are the honest options. Tutoring squeezed into a week with no room collapses by the third session, and that is a waste of everyone's effort.

faqs.question: Should a student moving from an Indian board into the Diploma prepare over the summer?
faqs.answer: A short block is worth more than a long one. The gap is marking conventions and the language of the criteria rather than content, so four to six sessions explicitly on how extended answers are credited, what reflection and evaluation mean in a criterion, and how method marks work will do more than a full summer of general revision. Front-load it on question technique. Content gaps, where they exist, show up quickly once the student is in the course and can be addressed then.

faqs.question: What do you need from us before the first session?
faqs.answer: Three things. One recent marked script or report, so a specialist can see where marks were actually lost. The board and syllabus code, plus the tier for Cambridge subjects. And a list of the support the school already provides, which is the question almost nobody asks and the one that most often saves money in this district. With those, the first session is a diagnostic that ends in a written recommendation rather than an hour spent establishing basic facts.

dubai/oud-metha.closingHeading: Buy the gap the school cannot reach
dubai/oud-metha.closingBody: Oud Metha families start from a better position than most in Dubai. The schools are long-established and well-resourced, the journey home is short, and a 3:30pm session is genuinely available. The risk is not under-provision, it is duplication: paying a specialist rate for content the lunchtime clinic already covers while the real gap, a command verb misread for two years or a calculation that is not yet automatic, stays exactly where it was. Write down what the school gives you, send one marked script, take a short diagnostic block with a defined end, and judge it against the school's next assessment. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video.

intro.heading: The gap between what a Palm Jumeirah school teaches and what the student has to do alone
paragraphs: Palm Jumeirah has a well-off, internationally mobile residential population spread across the Shoreline apartments on the Trunk, the villa fronds from A through M, the Golden Mile, the Crescent hotels and residences, and the newer towers near Nakheel Mall and The Pointe. It has nurseries. It does not have a mainstream K-12 private school campus. Every school-age child on this island commutes off it, down a single trunk road, and comes back the same way in the afternoon.

That geography is the first half of the problem this page addresses. A Palm Jumeirah student at Dubai College, the American School of Dubai, GEMS Wellington International School in Al Sufouh, Dubai International Academy Al Barsha or Kings' School Dubai in Umm Suqeim is spending real time in a car or on a bus twice a day. The time available for independent study between arriving home and a reasonable bedtime is shorter here than the household income would suggest, and it is the independent study that the Diploma and IGCSE actually weigh.

The second half is the part parents discover late. A Diploma student's points do not come only from examined papers. Each of six subjects carries an internally assessed component marked by the teacher against published criteria and moderated by the IB. On top of that sit the Extended Essay at 4,000 words, the Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, and the CAS portfolio. None of these are taught in the way a syllabus topic is taught. They are set, explained, and then substantially self-managed across two years.

IGCSE students face a smaller version of the same thing. The examined content is taught thoroughly in most of the schools this island feeds. What is not taught, in any meaningful sense, is how to revise nine subjects simultaneously, how to read a mark scheme, how to allocate forty-five minutes across a paper, and how to notice that a practice answer earned four marks out of seven for reasons that are visible in the mark scheme. Students are told to revise. Very few are taught how.

This is why the most common request we get from Palm Jumeirah households is not content teaching. It is a specialist to work on one named component: a Chemistry internal assessment that needs a controllable research question, a mathematics exploration that has no mathematics in it yet, an Extended Essay with a research question too broad to answer in 4,000 words, or a set of mock scripts that need reading against the mark scheme line by line.

Everything on this page is delivered as one-to-one tuition over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; home visits are a service we provide only in India. For a family on the Palm, the practical consequence is that nobody has to drive down the Trunk twice more in an evening, and the student gets a specialist in the specific component rather than a generalist who happens to live on the island.
