sections.heading: Starting, and the order the work should happen in
paragraphs: The useful first message is not a request for a tutor. It is a list: the school, the subjects and levels, which components are outstanding, the school's own internal deadline for each, and the most recent marked piece of work. A supervision plan is built backwards from those deadlines, and without them the first session is spent gathering information you already had.

The sequence that works is diagnostic, then question design, then method or structure, then one draft response, then final checks. Most households here need four to six supervision hours per component rather than a weekly slot, and often need a weekly slot in only one subject alongside it. We will say which, and we will say if we think a component is too far gone for supervision to be the right purchase.

Three limits, stated before payment. We do not promise grades or points totals. We do not place tutors in homes in the UAE; delivery is one-to-one online, and if that is not acceptable we are the wrong provider. And we will not produce, edit to completion or supply any part of an assessed component, however late the deadline is or however the request is phrased.

One further note on sequencing, because the order matters more than the hours. Supervision bought before a question is defined saves far more time than supervision bought after data has been collected, since a badly framed question cannot be rescued by better writing. If you have to choose a single hour, spend it on the question. If you can afford a second, spend it on the method or the structure. The draft-response hour is the one most families buy first, and it is the one that would have been unnecessary if the first two had happened.

process.title: Send the deadline list
process.description: School, subjects and levels, every outstanding component, and the school's internal deadline for each. School deadlines sit weeks before anything a board publishes, and the plan is built backwards from them rather than from the examination session.

process.title: Diagnostic hour
process.description: One online session reviewing marked work and the current state of each component. The output is a written note saying which problem you actually have: missing content, undefined question, collected but unusable data, or a draft that answers a different question.

process.title: Match on the component, not the subject
process.description: Supervision needs someone who knows the criteria for that subject at that level. We match on that, say how long it will take, and tell you if the only available specialist works in a time zone that suits early mornings or late evenings.

process.title: Place the hours early
process.description: Four hours spread across question design, method review, draft response and final checks beat twelve hours in the last fortnight. Sessions are booked to the school's dates, with the draft-response hour scheduled after the student has written, not before.

process.title: Record and hand back
process.description: Each session produces a written note of what was discussed and what the student agreed to do next. The notes stay available to you and to the school on request, which is useful if any question about authenticity ever arises.

whyPoints.title: Built for the unsupervised half
whyPoints.description: Most tutoring is sold against classroom content. The components that decide an IB grade sit outside lessons, and supervision for them is a different service with different timing. This page exists because that is what households in this community actually ask for.

whyPoints.title: A boundary your child hears out loud
whyPoints.description: Tutors state in the first session what they will and will not do with assessed work. That conversation is protection for the student, because authentication failures fall on the candidate rather than on the person who was paid.

whyPoints.title: Specialists chosen on criteria knowledge
whyPoints.description: Supervision needs someone who knows the mark criteria for that subject at that level, not a generalist who is willing to drive out to Al Qudra Road. Online delivery is what makes that selection possible from this community.

whyPoints.title: Rates you can check
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page names who published it and when. Three of the six agencies ranking for these searches publish no price at all, so comparing a quote against a sourced band is something you can only do here.

whyPoints.title: Limits said in advance
whyPoints.description: No grade promises, no fabricated success statistics, no claim of accreditation from KHDA, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and no UAE office. Where a specialist is scarce or slow to match, you hear that before you pay rather than afterwards.

faqs.question: My son's lesson reports are good but his internal assessments are late. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Reports describe the taught half of the course, and internal assessments live in the other half. Six Diploma subjects carry six investigations, each needing fifteen to thirty independent hours, and none of that appears on a weekly homework sheet. A student can be doing everything asked of them in lessons and still have four unfinished components. The diagnosis is almost never weakness; it is that nobody scheduled the independent hours. Fixing it means working backwards from the school's own deadlines and placing specific tasks in specific weeks.

faqs.question: How many supervision hours does one internal assessment actually need?
faqs.answer: Four to six, placed at the right moments, is usually enough. One hour on narrowing the question until the variables are nameable, one on method or structure before any data is collected, one responding to a draft the student has written, and one on final checks against the criteria and the formatting requirements. Hours added in the last fortnight buy much less, because by then the data is fixed and the only remaining improvement is in the writing. Early hours change what the investigation can score; late hours only protect it.

faqs.question: Can my daughter use data from inside The Sustainable City for her investigation?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a genuine advantage. Primary data is what the analysis criteria reward and what most candidates struggle to obtain. Measurable options here include photovoltaic output against time of day, shaded versus unshaded surface temperature, greenhouse growth under controlled conditions, irrigation or greywater reuse, and recorded movement on car-free streets. Two conditions apply: she must get permission for anything measured on school or community property, and the method must describe exactly how readings were taken rather than implying precision the instruments did not have.

faqs.question: Why did a fortnight of revision not move my child's MYP grade?
faqs.answer: Because the task was probably weighted to criteria the revision never touched. Every MYP subject is assessed against four criteria, lettered A to D and marked out of eight, and a task sheet usually names which criteria it assesses. Memorising content prepares criterion A and leaves B, C and D where they were. The practical move is to read the task sheet, ask the teacher which criterion sits closest to a grade boundary, and prepare against that strand. Two marks on the right criterion can move a whole grade.

faqs.question: What is the hardest transition inside an IB continuum?
faqs.answer: Middle Years into the Diploma, by a wide margin. The MYP rewards process, reflection and extended communication; the Diploma rewards precision against command terms and tight analytical writing under timed conditions. Students who learned to write expansively write too much and too loosely in the first Diploma term, and their marks fall even though their understanding has not. It is predictable and therefore preparable: command-term discipline and timed practice in the first term of DP1 prevent most of the drop that otherwise shows up in the first mock.

faqs.question: Does a tutor ever write part of an Extended Essay?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider who offers to is describing malpractice. A supervisor has to authenticate the essay as the student's own work, and a finding against the submission falls on the candidate. What a tutor can legitimately do is explain the assessment criteria, challenge the research question until four thousand words can actually answer it, show how comparable published work was structured, read one draft the student has written and reply with questions, and check formatting and referencing requirements. The writing, the argument and the sources remain the student's.

faqs.question: How do MYP criterion marks turn into a 1 to 7 grade?
faqs.answer: The four criterion marks, each out of eight, are added to give a total out of thirty-two, and that total is converted using grade boundaries published for each subject group. The consequence worth knowing is that movement is uneven: a student sitting just below a boundary may need two extra marks on one criterion to gain a whole grade, while a student at the top of a band can gain six marks and move nothing. Asking which criterion is nearest a boundary turns an anxious conversation into a defined piece of work.

faqs.question: Is Theory of Knowledge actually teachable?
faqs.answer: Yes, more than students assume. The essay is on a prescribed title and the marks go to a controlled structure: a precise interpretation of the title, claims supported by real examples, genuine counterclaims, and evaluation rather than assertion. That structure is coachable in a handful of sessions. The exhibition needs three objects linked to one prompt with a written commentary explaining how each connects, which is mostly a selection problem. Both fail for the same reason, which is being left until the term everything else is due.

faqs.question: What does equivalency require from a British-curriculum leaver?
faqs.answer: Five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited Advanced Level subject at no lower than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. A competitor page ranking for these searches claims six subjects are required, which is wrong. For the IB, no points threshold appears in the source behind those figures, so check moe.gov.ae or the attestation authority directly rather than relying on a tutoring site.

faqs.question: Do tutors visit villas on Al Qudra Road?
faqs.answer: IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE. Every lesson here is one-to-one over live video; home visiting is a service we operate only in India. For component supervision the screen is genuinely better: the criteria, the draft, the data file and the subject guide are visible to both people at once, and each session leaves a written record of what was discussed. A visiting tutor would also have to be someone willing to drive out at five in the afternoon, which removes most of the specialists from the choice.

faqs.question: What should a Diploma student have finished by the end of DP1?
faqs.answer: Enough that DP2 is about papers rather than paperwork. Realistically that means a defined Extended Essay research question with a supervisor meeting behind it, at least one internal assessment with data collected and analysed, a clear plan for the remaining investigations, Theory of Knowledge title shortlisted, and CAS reflections written as the activities happened rather than reconstructed later. Schools publish their own internal deadlines for most of this, and those dates, not the board's, are the ones a plan has to respect.

faqs.question: Can one tutor supervise two components in different subjects?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, with caution. The generic skills overlap: narrowing a question, defining variables, structuring an argument, reading criteria carefully. The specific marking does not, because the criteria and their strands differ by subject and level. For two investigations in related sciences a single specialist often works. For a maths exploration and a history essay it rarely does, and the right answer is two people for a small number of hours each rather than one person stretched across both.

faqs.question: Are lessons available during Ramadan and the summer break?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing changed. During Ramadan school days are shortened and most households move sessions to after Iftar, which suits Diploma students working on components at night. Over the long summer, families travelling out of the UAE often keep a reduced schedule online from wherever they are, which is one practical benefit of video delivery. The weeks worth protecting are those immediately before mocks and before an examination series, and those get agreed in advance rather than cancelled late.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to send if we want to start?
faqs.answer: A deadline list. The school, each subject and level, every outstanding component, the school's internal deadline for each, and the most recent marked piece of work. That lets a supervision plan be built backwards from real dates in the first hour rather than the third. If you can add the task sheet or criteria document the school issued, better again, because the plan then names strands rather than subjects and the first session starts with work instead of questions.

faqs.question: What will IB Gram refuse to do?
faqs.answer: We will not write, rewrite, edit to completion or supply any part of an assessed component, however close the deadline is. We will not promise a grade or a points total. We will not send anyone to a UAE address, because delivery here is online only. We hold no accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson and will not imply otherwise, and we do not perform or guarantee equivalency, which is a matter for the Ministry and the attestation authority.

dubai/the-sustainable-city.closingHeading: Work backwards from the school's deadlines
dubai/the-sustainable-city.closingBody: If your child is in the Diploma or the final MYP year, the most useful hour you can buy is one spent mapping every outstanding component against the school's own internal dates. That usually shows that two components need urgent attention, two need a question narrowed, and the rest need nothing yet. Send the deadline list and the last marked piece of work and we will say what the sequence should be, how many supervision hours it needs, and which weekly subject slot, if any, is worth adding. Where the honest answer is that a component is a school conversation rather than a tutoring purchase, we will tell you that instead.

dubai/the-valley.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work with primary and lower-secondary students as well as examination classes. For a younger child we match on patience and diagnostic skill first, then on subject, because the hard part at that age is finding out what is actually missing.

intro.heading: A young community, and a question with no number attached to it
paragraphs: The Valley is an Emaar community of townhouses and villas strung along the Dubai to Al Ain road, in phases named Eden, Nara, Talia, Elora, Alana and Rivana. Almost everything about the household profile follows from the housing: three-bedroom and four-bedroom homes bought by families at the start of their school years rather than at the end. The result is a community where primary-age children heavily outnumber sixth formers, and where the typical tutoring question is about a seven-year-old rather than a Diploma candidate. Emaar has announced schooling for the community, but for now the school run leaves it.

That changes the problem completely. A Year 12 parent has marks, mock papers and a syllabus to argue about. A Year 2 parent has a report describing their child as a confident communicator who is developing as an inquirer, and no idea whether that means fine or not fine. Primary reporting in both the International Baccalaureate Primary Years Programme and the English national curriculum has moved deliberately away from numbers, for sound educational reasons, and the side effect is that parents cannot see a gap opening.

Gaps at this stage are cheap to close and expensive to ignore. A child who never fully automated multiplication facts copes through Year 5, slows in Year 6, and hits a wall in algebra two years later, at which point the diagnosis looks like weakness in algebra. A child whose reading age sits two years behind their chronological age will struggle in science and humanities long before anyone describes it as a reading problem. Both are straightforward to measure and both are routinely missed.

The second thing The Valley has in common is distance. There is no large established secondary school inside the community, so children travel: north-west towards Dubailand and Mira, or towards the Nad Al Sheba and Meydan schools. For a six-year-old on a bus, that journey is the dominant fact of the afternoon, and it rules out most of the window in which a young child can concentrate. Online delivery at 16:00 from the kitchen table is a different proposition from a tutor arriving at 17:30.

This page is therefore built for the younger half of the community. It covers what a primary report hides, which standardised tests Dubai schools administer and how to read the results, what happens at the Year 6 to Year 7 handover and at the move from the Primary Years Programme into the Middle Years Programme, how early gaps compound into IGCSE problems, what intervention costs now against rescue later, how online lessons work for a child under eleven, and what the mandatory UAE subjects add to a young week. Every lesson runs online. IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE; that service exists only in India.

dubai/the-valley.programmesIntro: Three stages matter to this community, and only one of them involves public examinations. The notes below describe what each stage reports and what it conceals.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, organised around transdisciplinary units, and reported in terms of approaches to learning rather than attainment percentages. Children present an exhibition in the final year, which is usually their first extended independent project. Strong programmes develop research and thinking habits that pay off in the Diploma, but the reporting makes year-on-year arithmetic and literacy progress hard for a parent to track.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai PYP schools also teach Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies to every pupil under KHDA requirements, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab children. For a Valley family that is real timetable time, and it is the part of a primary week parents most often discover only when a report arrives with an Arabic grade on it.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The first stage where a child sees subject grades. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, lettered A to D and marked out of eight, with the total converted to a 1 to 7 grade using published boundaries. Parents moving from PYP reports to MYP grades frequently misread a 4 or 5 as a failure, when the scale does not work that way.
programmes.countryNote: Few Valley families have an MYP school inside the community, so the first two MYP years usually coincide with a long bus journey and a new timetable at once. The combination explains a dip in MYP 1 that is often mistaken for an academic problem when it is a logistics and workload problem.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Where primary gaps finally surface as grades. Cambridge codes subjects in four digits, with a Core and Extended split that fixes the grade ceiling before a student sits a paper; Pearson Edexcel uses codes such as 4MA1 and offers modular entry on some subjects. The arithmetic fluency and reading comprehension assumed by both were supposed to be settled years earlier.
programmes.countryNote: The British-curriculum schools this community feeds into use both boards, and a few departments use one for mathematics and another for sciences. The syllabus code on the entry slip, not the school's reputation, decides which past papers are worth a student's time in Year 11.

dubai/the-valley.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects The Valley households request, weighted towards the younger end. The description in each case is the specific skill being measured rather than a syllabus heading.

subjects.name: Primary mathematics
subjects.description: Number fluency, place value, fractions and the written methods a school expects. The common gap is recall speed rather than understanding: a child who can work out seven eights but takes four seconds to do it will run out of time in every later topic that uses it.

subjects.name: Primary English and reading
subjects.description: Decoding, fluency, comprehension and writing at length. Reading age is the single most useful measurement at this stage, because a gap of eighteen months quietly limits performance in science, humanities and word problems in mathematics well before it looks like a reading issue.

subjects.name: Lower secondary mathematics
subjects.description: Negative numbers, fractions to algebra, ratio and early geometry. Almost every difficulty in Year 8 algebra traces back to fractions and times tables, which is why a diagnostic at this stage looks backwards before it looks forwards.

subjects.name: Lower secondary science
subjects.description: The first time children must write explanations rather than descriptions, and the first time graph work is marked properly. Marks go missing on axis choice, units and the difference between a result and a conclusion rather than on the science itself.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: The Core and Extended decision sets a grade ceiling, and it is often taken in Year 9 on the basis of Year 8 performance. Students lose marks for unshown method and for misreading the demand of a question rather than for not knowing the topic.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Directed writing and reading comprehension at speed. Students who read little in primary school arrive here with the content knowledge but without the stamina to read a long unseen passage accurately under timed conditions.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: Three sciences in a compressed award, which punishes gaps rather than rewarding depth. Students who were never confident with rearranging formulae in Year 9 lose the same marks repeatedly across physics and chemistry papers.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, and children who join Dubai schooling after Year 3 often need script and vocabulary work the timetable cannot pace for them.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Included because Valley parents ask about it early. Reasoning marks dominate, so a correct answer with no justification scores a fraction of the available credit, and the course assumes algebraic fluency that was built or not built in Years 7 to 9.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy and command-term sensitive. Students who revise by rereading rather than answering are the ones who lose marks, and the habit forms in lower secondary where nobody insists on precision in written answers.

dubai/the-valley.regionsIntro: The Valley sits at the eastern end of a long line of Dubailand communities. What each neighbouring area changes is the length of the bus route and therefore the hour at which a young child can still concentrate.

regions.name: Mudon
regions.note: Along the same belt with its own primary provision. The practical difference for tutoring is that Mudon children are usually home earlier, so a Valley household with a friend's timetable in mind should expect a later slot than theirs.

regions.name: DAMAC Hills 2 and Dubailand residence communities

sections.heading: What a primary report tells you, and what it leaves out
paragraphs: Primary reporting in Dubai has moved, deliberately and almost universally, away from numbers. A Primary Years Programme report describes a child against learner attributes and approaches to learning. An English national curriculum report in a Dubai school typically uses working towards, working at and working above the expected standard, sometimes with an effort grade alongside. Both are defensible pieces of educational practice and both are nearly useless as a gap detector for a parent, because they compress a two-year range into one phrase.

Consider what working at the expected standard covers. It covers a child comfortably in the middle of the year group and a child at the very bottom of the band who will slip below it next term. It covers a child whose arithmetic is slow but accurate and a child whose arithmetic is fast but whose reading is eighteen months behind. The phrase is true in all four cases and tells you nothing about which one you have, which is why so many Valley parents arrive at a tutoring conversation unable to describe the problem.

The way through is to ask for the underlying data rather than the summary. Schools hold more than they report: reading ages, standardised test scores, book-band levels, and the teacher's own view of where a child sits inside the band. All of it is available on request at a parents' evening, and none of it is controversial to ask for. Two specific questions do most of the work: where in the band does my child sit, and what is their reading age against their actual age.

sections.heading: The standardised tests your child has probably already sat
paragraphs: Most Dubai private schools administer at least one standardised assessment a year from around Year 3 upwards, and many administer two. The families who find them most useful are the ones who ask for the results rather than waiting for them to appear on a report, because the numbers answer precisely the question that the written report avoids. The common instruments are cognitive ability tests, subject progress tests in English, mathematics and science, growth measures administered twice a year, and standalone reading tests.

A percentile or standardised score needs reading carefully. A standardised score is set so that one hundred is average for a child of that exact age, with most children between roughly eighty-five and one hundred and fifteen. A percentile says how many children out of a hundred scored lower. The trap is treating these as a verdict on ability: a cognitive score measures reasoning on the day, under test conditions, in English, which systematically understates children still acquiring the language of instruction.

The genuinely useful reading is comparative. A child whose reasoning score is well above their attainment score in mathematics is underperforming relative to their own capability, and that gap is a tutoring argument. A child whose attainment sits above their reasoning score is working hard and doing well, and more tutoring may be the wrong purchase. A child whose reading score lags both is telling you where the real constraint is. One conversation with the school asking for both numbers is worth more than a term of guesswork.

sections.heading: Year 6 into Year 7: the drop that is usually not academic
paragraphs: The move into Year 7, or into MYP 1, changes almost every condition a child has worked under. One teacher becomes ten. One classroom becomes a timetable with rooms and corridors. Homework arrives from several subjects on the same evening with different deadlines, and nobody checks a planner daily. Assessment becomes frequent and marked. For a Valley child this all coincides with a longer bus journey to a secondary school outside the community.

Marks fall in the first term for most children, and parents interpret the fall as an academic problem. Usually it is an organisational one. A child who could hold one teacher's expectations in their head cannot hold ten, and the work that suffers first is the work nobody reminded them about. The tell is a pattern of good test results and missing homework, or strong class participation and weak written output, rather than uniform weakness.

What helps is narrow and dull. A written weekly plan the child maintains themselves. A fixed time and place for homework. A habit of reading the task instructions aloud before starting. A checked bag the night before. For the minority whose problem genuinely is academic, the gap is almost always in arithmetic fluency or reading comprehension rather than in the new Year 7 content, which is why a diagnostic should look backwards at Years 4 to 6 before it looks at the current topic.

One specific piece of advice helps more than any other at this handover. Ask the school which members of staff are responsible for a Year 7 child who is struggling with organisation rather than with work, and contact that person early rather than waiting for a report. Form tutors and heads of year deal with exactly this problem every autumn, they have systems for it, and they are far more useful in October than in February. A paid tutor cannot check a planner daily; the school can, and asking is free.

sections.heading: The first time a child sees a grade, and what it actually means
paragraphs: Children who move from the Primary Years Programme into the Middle Years Programme meet numerical grades for the first time, and so do their parents. Each MYP subject is assessed against four criteria, lettered A to D and each marked out of eight. The four marks total thirty-two and convert to a grade from 1 to 7 using boundaries published for each subject group. A child who has only ever been described in words comes home with a 4 and a household panic starts.

A 4 is not a failure. On a seven-point scale with published descriptors, it describes adequate performance against demanding criteria, and the distance from a 4 to a 5 is frequently two or three marks spread across two criteria. The far more useful question is which criterion is furthest from its boundary, because that converts an anxious conversation into one concrete piece of work. Teachers can answer it immediately if asked.

The second thing to understand is that criteria differ by subject group. Criterion C in a science is not criterion C in a language, and a task is designed to assess some criteria and not others. A child who revises content for a task weighted towards communication will see no improvement and conclude that effort does not work, which is a far more damaging lesson than a 4. Reading the task sheet, which almost always names the criteria assessed, is the cheapest intervention available in the MYP.

sections.heading: How a Year 4 gap becomes an IGCSE grade
paragraphs: Two primary gaps compound more than any others, and both are measurable. The first is arithmetic automaticity. A child who computes rather than recalls number facts is spending working memory on arithmetic that a classmate spends on the actual problem. In Year 5 this costs a little speed. In Year 8 algebra it costs accuracy, because every manipulation carries an arithmetic step. By Year 11 it reads as weakness in algebra, and tutoring aimed at algebra will not fix it.

The second is reading. A reading age eighteen months behind chronological age does not announce itself as a reading problem. It announces itself as poor performance in science, where the questions are long, and in humanities, where the sources are dense, and in mathematics word problems, where the arithmetic is easy and the sentence is not. Fixing reading at nine is weeks of work. Compensating for it at fifteen, across six subjects with examinations approaching, is a different and much larger job.

The practical consequence for a Valley household is that the cheapest intervention available is also the earliest. A diagnostic hour at eight or nine, acted on with ten minutes of daily practice, closes gaps that cost a term of paid tuition at fifteen. This is not an argument for tutoring every child from Year 2. It is an argument for measuring, once, so that the decision to act or to wait is made on a number rather than on a feeling.

sections.heading: What early work costs against what late rescue costs
paragraphs: Market rates in Dubai are published by a handful of providers and withheld by most. The figures below were collected in October 2026, with the publisher named in each row, and they are market rates rather than an IB Gram price list. What they show is that primary support and examination-year specialist teaching are not the same purchase at all, and pricing them as if they were is how families end up overspending at the wrong end.

A young child needs short sessions, which means the hourly rate matters less than the session length and frequency. Two thirty-minute blocks a week at the qualified-tutor band costs less in a term than one specialist hour a week, and does more for a seven-year-old, because fluency work rewards frequency over duration. An examination-year student needs the opposite: longer sessions with a specialist who knows the board and the mark scheme, which is the band where rates climb.

There is one more figure worth knowing. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package worth AED 1.5 billion. Tuition is therefore the movable part of this year's education spend. For a community with as many primary children as The Valley, the highest-return use of it is a single diagnostic followed by a small, consistent amount of work, rather than a large block of hours bought in a year when examinations are still six years away.

sections.heading: Online lessons for a child under eleven: what actually works
paragraphs: Parents reasonably ask whether a seven-year-old can learn on a video call. The answer is yes, under conditions that are different from those for a teenager, and worse if those conditions are ignored. Session length is the first: thirty to forty-five minutes, not an hour. A young child's useful attention on a screen runs out well before an hour does, and the last fifteen minutes of a long session undo some of the first thirty.

The second condition is that the session has one objective, stated at the start and checked at the end. Vague sessions that drift across topics fail at this age in a way they do not with an examination candidate who can hold a purpose themselves. The third is that a parent sits within earshot for the first few sessions, not to teach but so the child knows the arrangement is taken seriously and so you can see what is actually happening.

The fourth is practice between sessions, measured in minutes rather than worksheets. Five to ten minutes of timed number facts or reading aloud, daily, outperforms a weekend hour. The reason is the same reason that makes video delivery practical here: for this community the alternative is a tutor driving the Dubai to Al Ain road at five in the afternoon, arriving at the exact moment a tired child has least left to give. IB Gram does not place tutors in UAE homes in any case, and a 16:00 start from the kitchen table is a better hour than a 17:45 one.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies in a young child's week
paragraphs: Every private school in Dubai teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of the international curriculum it is licensed to deliver, and KHDA set a requirement that these arrangements be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For a Valley family this is often the part of the week they understand least, and the part that produces the first unexpected grade on a primary report.

The rules are specific. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, and Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils, while non-Arab pupils are taught Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

Two further details help a parent plan. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory subject lesson be at least twenty-five minutes. Schools are also required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects. And because the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited for these subjects, tutoring here is about access to the school's own material and the language skills to use it, not about an alternative syllabus.

sections.heading: Starting with a young child, and when the answer is to do nothing
paragraphs: The first step costs one hour and often saves a term of fees. Send the most recent report, any standardised test result the school has issued, and one piece of marked work. Then book a single diagnostic session. The tutor checks arithmetic recall against the clock and reading accuracy against a graded passage, compares both with the school's own numbers, and writes down what was found.

A meaningful proportion of those sessions end with a recommendation to do nothing. A child who is inside the normal range, whose reasoning and attainment scores agree, and whose reading age matches their chronological age does not need paid tuition; they need time and a library card. Any provider who never reaches that conclusion is not diagnosing. We would rather tell you to wait a term and come back than sell a year of lessons a seven-year-old does not need.

Where work is warranted, expect it to be narrow, short and frequent: thirty or forty-five minute sessions, one objective each, five to ten minutes of daily practice, and a review against measurable numbers rather than against impressions after six weeks. Three limits are worth stating in advance. We make no promises about grades or test scores. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, as every lesson is one-to-one online. And we hold no accreditation or partnership from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and will not suggest otherwise.

process.title: Ask the school for the numbers
process.description: Before contacting any tutor, request your child's reading age, their most recent standardised scores, and where in the attainment band the teacher places them. All three are routinely available and none is awkward to ask for at a parents' evening.

process.title: One diagnostic session
process.description: Thirty to sixty minutes online depending on age, spent measuring rather than teaching: timed number-fact recall, a graded reading passage, and one piece of written work reviewed with the child. You receive a written summary of what was found.

process.title: Decide to act or to wait
process.description: The summary says which it should be. Where scores, reading age and classroom performance agree and sit in range, waiting a term is the right answer and we will say so. Where they disagree, the summary names the specific gap to work on.

process.title: Short sessions, one objective each
process.description: For primary children, thirty or forty-five minutes once or twice weekly, with five to ten minutes of daily practice in between. Each session opens by naming its objective and closes by checking it, which is what keeps a young child's hour from drifting.

process.title: Review against the same measures
process.description: After six weeks, the same timed recall and the same style of reading check are repeated. Progress is a change in those numbers, not an impression that lessons are going well. If nothing moved, the diagnosis or the tutor changes rather than the hours increasing.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to wait when waiting is right
whyPoints.description: A real diagnostic sometimes concludes that a child is fine and needs time rather than tuition. A provider who reaches that conclusion occasionally is measuring something; one who never does is selling. This matters more at primary age than at any other stage.

whyPoints.title: Measurement instead of impressions
whyPoints.description: Reading age, timed number-fact recall and the school's own standardised scores give you a number where the report gives you a phrase. Decisions about a seven-year-old should rest on those numbers rather than on a parent's worry or a teacher's kind sentence.

whyPoints.title: Session length matched to age
whyPoints.description: Thirty minutes twice a week beats an hour once a week for a child under eleven, because fluency responds to frequency. Most tutoring is sold in hour blocks because hours are easy to bill, not because they suit young children.

whyPoints.title: The right hour, not the hour a car can reach
whyPoints.description: The useful window for a Valley child sits straight after the bus and before they are too tired. Online delivery can take a 16:00 slot. A visiting tutor driving the Dubai to Al Ain road at peak cannot, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE in any case.

whyPoints.title: No invented numbers, no promises
whyPoints.description: We publish no success rates, no satisfaction percentages and no grade guarantees, and every AED figure on this page names who published it. We hold no accreditation from KHDA, the Ministry of Education or any examination board and will not imply one.

faqs.question: My daughter's PYP report has no grades. How do I tell if she is behind?
faqs.answer: Ask the school for three things the report leaves out: her reading age against her actual age, her most recent standardised test scores, and where inside the attainment band her teacher places her. All three exist and are routinely shared at a parents' evening. A report phrase like working at the expected standard spans a very wide range, covering both a child comfortably mid-year-group and one about to slip below. The numbers distinguish between those two cases; the phrase cannot.

faqs.question: What does a standardised score of 100 actually mean?
faqs.answer: Standardised scores are set so that 100 is the average for a child of that exact age, with most children falling roughly between 85 and 115. A percentile instead tells you how many children in a hundred scored below your child. Neither is a verdict on ability. Cognitive tests in particular measure reasoning on one day, under test conditions, in English, which systematically understates children still acquiring the language of instruction. The useful reading is comparative rather than absolute.

faqs.question: Why would a reasoning score be higher than a maths score?
faqs.answer: Because the two measure different things, and the gap between them is the most informative number a parent can get. A reasoning score well above an attainment score means a child is capable of more than they are currently producing, which is the clearest argument for intervention there is. Attainment above reasoning usually means a child is working hard and doing well, and extra tutoring may be the wrong purchase. If a reading score lags both, reading is the constraint and should be fixed first.

faqs.question: Is thirty minutes long enough for a tutoring session at seven?
faqs.answer: For most seven-year-olds it is the right length, and an hour is actively worse. Useful attention on a screen at that age runs out well before sixty minutes, and the final stretch of a long session can undo gains from the start. Thirty minutes twice a week with five to ten minutes of daily practice in between does more for arithmetic fluency and reading than one weekly hour, because both respond to frequency rather than duration. Longer sessions become appropriate from around Year 7.

faqs.question: My son's marks dropped in Year 7. Should I be worried?
faqs.answer: Probably not yet, and probably not about academics. Year 7 replaces one teacher with ten, adds a timetable, and sends homework from several subjects on the same evening with nobody checking a planner daily. Most children dip in the first term for organisational reasons. The tell is a pattern: good test results with missing homework points to organisation, while uniformly weak work across subjects points to a real gap, usually in arithmetic fluency or reading rather than in new Year 7 content.

faqs.question: Why did my child get a 4 in MYP after years of good primary reports?
faqs.answer: Because the scale changed, not the child. Each MYP subject is marked against four criteria lettered A to D, each out of eight, totalling thirty-two, which converts to a 1 to 7 grade using published boundaries. A 4 describes adequate performance against demanding criteria, and the distance to a 5 is often two or three marks spread across two criteria. Ask the teacher which criterion sits furthest from its boundary; that single answer turns a worrying grade into one defined piece of work.

faqs.question: How early can slow times tables cause a real problem?
faqs.answer: The cost starts invisibly and becomes visible around Year 8. A child who computes rather than recalls number facts spends working memory on arithmetic that a fluent classmate spends on the problem itself. In primary that shows as slow completion with correct answers. In algebra it shows as errors, because every manipulation carries an arithmetic step. By Year 11 it reads as weakness in algebra, and tutoring aimed at algebra will not repair it. Fixing recall takes weeks at nine and a term at fifteen.

faqs.question: Does a reading problem affect subjects other than English?
faqs.answer: Heavily, and usually before anyone calls it a reading problem. A reading age eighteen months behind chronological age shows up as poor science performance, because the questions are long, as difficulty with humanities sources, and as failure on mathematics word problems where the arithmetic is simple and the sentence is not. That is why reading age is the single highest-value measurement available at primary level, and why it is worth fixing before anything else when it is behind.

faqs.question: Which standardised tests do Dubai schools usually run?
faqs.answer: Most private schools here administer at least one a year from around Year 3: a cognitive ability test measuring verbal, non-verbal, quantitative and spatial reasoning, a subject progress test in English, mathematics or science, a twice-yearly growth measure, and often a standalone reading test. Schools vary, so ask yours by name. The results are usually held whether or not they are reported, and requesting them is routine rather than an imposition on the teacher.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our townhouse in The Valley?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram runs home visits only in India; every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. For this community that is the better arrangement on timing alone. A visiting tutor would be driving the Dubai to Al Ain road at the worst hour and arriving around 17:45, which is when a young child has least concentration left. An online session can start at 16:00, straight after the bus, in the half-hour when a seven-year-old can still do useful work.

faqs.question: What do the mandatory UAE subjects add to a primary week?
faqs.answer: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are taught in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed international curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, prohibits combined classes for those subjects, and calculates instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit while advising at least twenty-five minutes for any mandatory lesson. For most Valley families that is several periods a week, and it explains the first grade on a primary report that parents did not expect to see.

faqs.question: Can we tutor the mandatory Arabic curriculum directly?
faqs.answer: Support is about access rather than replacement. For these subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so the work is on the language skills and study habits a child needs to use the school's own material: script fluency, vocabulary, listening and the confidence to answer in Arabic. That is particularly relevant for non-Arab children who joined Dubai schooling after Year 3 and are being paced against classmates who started in Year 1.

faqs.question: How soon would we know whether tutoring is working?
faqs.answer: Six weeks, measured against the same checks used at the start. For a primary child that means repeating the timed number-fact recall and a comparable graded reading passage, and comparing the numbers rather than the impressions. For a secondary student it means a marked piece of work from school rather than from the tutor. If the numbers have not moved, the right response is to change the diagnosis or the tutor, not to add hours to an arrangement that is not working.

faqs.question: Which documents make a first diagnostic session worth paying for?
faqs.answer: Three documents and one date. The most recent school report, any standardised test result the school has issued, and one piece of marked work, plus the date of the next assessment if there is one. For a Year 10 or 11 student add the exact syllabus code from the examination entry. Those items let the diagnostic hour be spent measuring and teaching rather than collecting information, which is the difference between a useful first session and an expensive questionnaire.

faqs.question: What will IB Gram not claim or do?
faqs.answer: We make no promises about grades, test scores or percentile movement, and publish no success statistics, because none of ours would carry a sample size, a date and a method. We do not place tutors in homes anywhere in the UAE. We hold no accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson and will not imply one. And we will not recommend paid lessons for a child whose own numbers say they do not need them.

dubai/the-valley.closingHeading: Get the number before you buy the hours
dubai/the-valley.closingBody: If your child is in primary or lower secondary, the most valuable thing you can do this term is not book a tutor. Ask the school for their reading age and their latest standardised scores, then book one diagnostic hour online to check arithmetic recall and reading accuracy directly. That gives you a number instead of a worry, and it is the only honest basis for deciding whether to act. Where the numbers say your child is fine, we will tell you to wait a term. Where they point to a specific gap, the work is short, narrow and frequent, and it is far cheaper now than the same gap will be in Year 11.

dubai/the-views.heroSubtitle: IB and IGCSE tutors in The Views exist to cover the half of the grade a school timetable cannot reach. The Views looks out over Emirates Golf Club, and the students in Panorama, Travo, Turia and the Fairways towers attend good schools that teach the syllabus well. What those schools cannot do is sit with one child through a 4,000-word essay, an internal assessment and eight past papers. That work is independent by design, and it is where grades move.

dubai/the-views.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched to a component rather than a subject: a scientific investigation, a mathematics exploration, a prescribed-title essay, a Paper 3. Supervision of independent work is a different skill from teaching a class, and it is the one The Views asks for most.

intro.heading: The gap between the hours a school teaches and the hours that earn the grade
paragraphs: Count the taught hours in a Diploma subject and compare them with what the final grade is built from. A Higher Level subject gets perhaps four or five periods a week across two years. Inside that time a teacher has to deliver a demanding syllabus to a class of twenty with mixed prior attainment. What the teacher cannot do, because the arithmetic forbids it, is work through one student's internal assessment line by line against five criteria, or mark eight full past papers for one candidate and talk through every lost mark.

That is not a criticism of the schools The Views families use. Regent International School sits minutes away in The Greens, Emirates International School Meadows runs the full IB continuum, and Dubai College and GEMS Wellington International School in Al Sufouh take a large share of the older students here. These are well-run schools doing the job a school is structured to do. The point is narrower: a significant and specified fraction of both the Diploma and IGCSE is assessed on work the student produces outside taught time, and nobody is timetabled to supervise it.

For the Diploma the numbers make this unarguable. Every subject carries an internally assessed component, typically worth a fifth to a quarter of the subject grade, marked by the teacher against published criteria and moderated by the IB. On top of that sit three core components with no subject class at all: a 4,000-word extended essay supervised by a teacher in occasional meetings, a Theory of Knowledge exhibition and prescribed-title essay, and Creativity, Activity, Service. None of those is lesson content. All of them have deadlines.

For IGCSE the independent half looks different and matters just as much. The content is taught; the marks are lost in execution. Command terms, working shown, units, significant figures, the discipline of answering the question asked instead of the question revised for. A student who has worked twelve past papers under timed conditions with the mark scheme open afterwards performs differently from one who has read the textbook three times, and the twelve papers are not timetabled either.

The Views is a small community of mid-rise towers with mostly one or two children per household, which means families here tend to have time and attention for one child's workload in a way a three-child villa does not. That is an advantage, and it is usually spent on the wrong thing - helping with content the school already covered rather than supervising the independent work the school cannot. Reallocating that attention is most of what good tutoring does in this neighbourhood.

The practical test of whether a family has the balance right is a short one. Ask what the student worked on last weekend. If the answer is reading notes or watching revision videos, the attention is going into content. If the answer is a timed paper that somebody then marked, or a paragraph of an investigation rewritten after reading the criterion descriptor, the attention is going into the half of the grade that is actually unclaimed. The second answer is rarer than it should be in a community where the schools are this capable.

dubai/the-views.programmesIntro: Each route leaves a different share of the grade to independent work, and that share is what a family should be buying support for. Below is how much of each programme happens outside taught time, and who supervises it when it does.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher and Standard Level plus three core components. The internally assessed element in each subject is produced by the student, marked by the teacher against published criteria and moderated externally by the IB. The written papers sit in the May session Dubai schools use, but the internal deadlines a school sets for coursework fall across DP1 and the first half of DP2, which is why the heaviest workload is not the one closest to the exams.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students from The Views are concentrated at Emirates International School Meadows and GEMS Dubai American Academy, with a share at Dubai International Academy Emirates Hills. Each school publishes its own internal assessment calendar, and those calendars differ by weeks. A plan built from a generic Diploma timeline rather than from the student's own school calendar will be wrong, usually in the direction of starting late.

programmes.name: Extended essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS
programmes.description: The extended essay is a 4,000-word independent research piece in a subject of the student's choosing, supervised by a school teacher in a limited number of recorded meetings. Theory of Knowledge is assessed through an exhibition with written commentaries and an essay on a title prescribed by the IB. Creativity, Activity, Service is a portfolio requirement with reflections rather than a graded component. Together the essay and Theory of Knowledge contribute points to the Diploma total.
programmes.countryNote: This is the single largest source of late-term distress among The Views families, and it is entirely predictable. A student who chooses an extended essay question in the first term of DP1 has eighteen months. One who chooses in June has a summer and a panic. Supervision here is process work: narrowing the question, confirming sources exist, building a timeline against the school's checkpoints, and reading drafts the student has written.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal written papers in eight to ten subjects, with syllabus codes that determine the paper structure: Cambridge 0580, 0625, 0620, 0610 and their Pearson Edexcel counterparts such as 4MA1 and 4PH1. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, capping the available grade at Core. Practical science is examined either through a practical test or an alternative-to-practical paper at Cambridge, and inside the theory papers at Pearson.
programmes.countryNote: The independent work at this level is past-paper practice and mark-scheme literacy, and almost no family does it systematically without help. A Year 11 in The Views who works one paper a week from October, timed, and spends the following session on the mark scheme will have covered the question types twice over by February. The constraint is not ability; it is that nobody is checking the papers get done.

programmes.name: A Level, the route after IGCSE
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, assessed by written papers with practical endorsement in the sciences. Content depth per subject exceeds Higher Level IB in several cases, while breadth is far narrower and there is no equivalent of the Diploma core. Independent work here is dominated by past papers, extended written response and, in the sciences, the practical endorsement record a student maintains across two years.
programmes.countryNote: Regent International School and Dubai College both take students through to A Level, and The Views sends children to each. The decision between A Level and the Diploma is generally made in Year 11 and is worth one properly informed conversation: three subjects in depth suits a decided student, and six subjects plus core suits one who has not yet chosen a direction.

dubai/the-views.subjectsIntro: The requests from The Views cluster around components rather than subjects: an exploration that is stuck, a scientific investigation with no usable data, a Paper 3 nobody has practised. What follows is the independent element in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Two written papers at Standard Level, three at Higher, plus the mathematical exploration marked out of 20 against five criteria. Explorations fail on scope rather than on mathematics: a question too broad to answer in the page count, or too narrow to show use of mathematics at the right level. Fixing scope early costs one session and saves a term.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator assumed throughout. The exploration rewards a genuine dataset and a real question. Invented or scraped-and-unexamined data is visible to a moderator within a page, and the reflection criterion is where students who collected real data pull clear of those who did not.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The scientific investigation is marked out of 24 across research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. Most lost marks sit in evaluation: a student who reports what happened but cannot say what limited the method loses a whole criterion. Uncertainty propagation and significant figures are mechanical marks that go missing through habit.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, waves and energy with heavy algebraic demand at Higher Level, plus the scientific investigation. Independent work here is dominated by multi-step derivation under time pressure, which cannot be learned from reading. Paper 3 style data analysis on an unfamiliar experiment is the component students most reliably under-practise.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Precision of command-term response decides the grade more than breadth of recall. An investigation needs a controlled variable set a student can defend and enough repeats to support a statistical claim. Data-based questions on experiments the student has never seen reward practice against past papers rather than revision of notes.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source-based and essay papers plus the historical investigation, which asks for a question, source evaluation and reflection on method. Students lose marks by narrating rather than arguing, and by evaluating sources in the abstract instead of against the specific question. The investigation is the most teachable research skill in the Diploma.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Written papers with an internally assessed fieldwork report built on primary data the student collects. The report fails when data collection was not designed around a hypothesis, which is a planning problem rather than a writing one. Higher Level adds a third paper on global interactions.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches, with an experimental study written up as the internal assessment. Ethical constraints shape what a student may investigate, and most rejected proposals fall over on ethics rather than on method. Command-term precision carries more marks here than most students expect.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Two written papers, the individual oral, and at Higher Level an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on a studied work. The individual oral asks for a global issue argued through two extracts, and students arrive with a theme instead of an issue more often than not. That distinction is the single highest-value hour in the course.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Power, human rights, development and peace, with an engagement activity written up against a political issue the student investigates directly. The written component rewards a tight political question and sinks under a broad topic, so scope work at the planning stage is the whole job.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An exhibition of three objects with written commentaries, and an essay on one of the IB's prescribed titles. The essay is marked on the quality of its argument about knowledge, not on subject content, which is why strong subject students frequently underperform on it. It is coachable and almost never practised.

dubai/the-views.regionsTitle: The Views and the communities it shares a school run with
dubai/the-views.regionsIntro: Towers in The Views sit between Sheikh Zayed Road, Hessa Street and the golf course, and the school runs out of here cross several communities. Each neighbour changes the realistic session window.

regions.name: The Greens
regions.note: Immediately next door and home to Regent International School, which many Views children walk or are driven to in minutes. Those households can hold a 3.45pm slot, which is unusually early for Dubai and useful for younger students.

regions.name: The Lakes
regions.note: Villas across the community, with more multi-child households and therefore more staggered slots. Views families often share carpools here, which ties the two communities' pickup times together.

regions.name: The Meadows
regions.note: Emirates International School Meadows and its full IB continuum sit here. Most of the extended essay and internal assessment supervision requested from The Views is timed against that school's published internal calendar.

regions.name: Al Sufouh
regions.note: Dubai College and GEMS Wellington International School. The drive crosses Al Sufouh Road twice a day, which removes anything before 5.00pm from the week for families with a child at either.

regions.name: Emirates Hills
regions.note: Large villas north of the golf course, with Dubai International Academy Emirates Hills nearby. Requests from there are weighted towards minority Higher Level subjects and Theory of Knowledge supervision.

regions.name: Barsha Heights
regions.note: Minutes away and where a share of Views parents work. A short commute makes a 6.30pm session with a parent at home genuinely practical, which suits coursework supervision better than a rushed afternoon slot.

regions.name: Dubai Internet City
regions.note: The metro station and office cluster at the edge of the community. Students who travel independently by metro have more scheduling freedom than those who depend on a parent driving, and the plan should use that.

regions.name: Jumeirah Lake Towers
regions.note: Across Sheikh Zayed Road, with its own apartment families and a shared social circle. Weekend morning blocks are popular across both communities because the interchange is quiet on a Saturday.

schoolClusters.city: The Greens, The Views and Emirates Living
schoolClusters.note: The nearby schools, covering the British route and the IB continuum. These are the schools whose published internal assessment calendars most supervision plans from The Views are built against.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh and Al Barsha
schoolClusters.note: Where most older students from The Views are enrolled. Longer commutes and later finishing times mean coursework supervision here is usually booked for the evening or for weekend mornings rather than straight after school.

dubai/the-views.modesIntro: Three formats cover the independent work, and they are chosen by which component is in trouble rather than by age or subject. All are delivered one-to-one over live video.

modes.title: Coursework supervision, timed to the school's checkpoints
modes.description: Sessions clustered around a school's own internal deadlines rather than spread evenly through the year. The sequence is the same every time: narrow the question, confirm the method or sources are workable, read the criteria together, then read a draft the student has written and say which criterion is underserved. Short, frequent and concentrated into the weeks before a checkpoint, with nothing between checkpoints.
bullets: Plan built from the school's published internal calendar
Criterion-by-criterion feedback on the student's own draft
Scope and feasibility settled before any writing begins
No wording supplied for submission, in any component

modes.title: Timed past-paper cycles
modes.description: A weekly cycle in which the student sits a paper under exam conditions, the tutor marks it against the published scheme, and the following session is spent only on the lost marks. This is the format that moves IGCSE and A Level grades without new content, and it works because somebody external is checking the paper actually got done. Twelve cycles between October and February covers the question types twice.
bullets: One timed paper a week, marked against the real scheme
Session spent on lost marks rather than on topics
Command terms and working-shown habits corrected in writing
Progress tracked as marks recovered per question type

modes.title: Theory of Knowledge and extended essay clinics
modes.description: Short, focused sessions on the two components with no subject class behind them. For Theory of Knowledge that means unpicking a prescribed title into a real knowledge question and testing whether the argument survives a counterclaim. For the extended essay it means a research question narrow enough to answer in 4,000 words and a timeline that lands before the school's deadline rather than on it.
bullets: Prescribed title broken into an arguable knowledge question
Counterclaims tested before the essay is drafted
Extended essay question checked for scope and available sources
Timeline mapped to the school's checkpoints, not to the exam

sections.heading: The Diploma core counted backwards from the school's own deadlines
paragraphs: The three core components are where capable students in The Views lose points, and the reason is structural rather than academic. There is no weekly class. A school assigns an extended essay supervisor who meets the student a handful of times, sets internal checkpoints, and otherwise relies on the student to manage eighteen months of independent research. Theory of Knowledge gets some timetabled time in most schools, but the exhibition and the essay are still produced alone.

The dates that govern this are set by the school, not by the IB, and they are published. A family that asks the Diploma coordinator for the internal assessment calendar in the first term of DP1 gets a document that makes the whole two years legible: when the extended essay question must be registered, when the first draft is due, when each subject's internal assessment is collected, when mocks run. Almost nobody asks for it, and the ones who do find the rest of the planning straightforward.

Working backwards from those checkpoints rather than forwards from today is what turns panic into a timetable. If a first full extended essay draft is due in May of DP1, then source gathering has to be finished by March, the research question settled by January, and the subject chosen by November. Each of those is a one-session conversation if it happens on time and a crisis if it happens three months late.

Specific IB session and results dates are a different matter and should not be taken from any tutoring page. Dubai schools sit the May session; the precise windows and results dates should be confirmed with the school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org. What a family can plan against with complete confidence is the school's own calendar, because the school sets it and publishes it.

sections.heading: Internal assessment criteria by letter, and where the marks actually sit
paragraphs: No competing page in this search names a single assessment criterion. That is a remarkable gap, because the criteria are the entire basis on which internal assessments are marked, they are published, and a student who has read them performs measurably differently from one who has not. Most students have seen the criteria once, at the point the task was set, and never read the descriptors.

Take the mathematics exploration, marked out of 20 across five criteria: presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics. The largest single allocation sits on use of mathematics, which is where a student who picks a question that is too easy caps their own mark however well they write it up. Personal engagement and reflection together carry a substantial share and are the two criteria most often treated as decoration. They are not decoration; they are marks with descriptors.

The sciences work differently again. The scientific investigation is marked out of 24 across research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation, in equal weight. Evaluation is where most students lose a full criterion, because reporting what happened is easier than identifying what limited the method and what a better design would have done. A student who writes an honest evaluation of a flawed experiment outscores one who writes a confident account of the same experiment.

The practical move is unglamorous and reliable. Before writing anything, the student reads the descriptor for the top band of each criterion and writes one sentence per criterion describing how their work will satisfy it. If they cannot write that sentence, the work is not ready. This takes twenty minutes, happens almost never, and is the single highest-return habit in Diploma coursework. Confirm the current mark allocations in your school's subject guide, since the IB revises them.

sections.heading: Word and page limits across assessment components
paragraphs: Limits are hard constraints, and students treat them as targets. The distinction matters because exceeding a limit is penalised in most components and because writing to a limit is a skill in itself. A reference table of these limits does not appear on any page competing for these searches, which is odd given that every Diploma student needs one and every one of them asks a teacher instead.

The reason the limits bite is that they force scope decisions early. A 4,000-word extended essay cannot answer a broad question, so the question has to be narrowed before research begins rather than after a first draft runs to 6,000 words and has to be cut. A student who writes 6,000 and cuts to 4,000 produces a worse essay than one who planned for 4,000, because the cutting removes evidence rather than padding.

Short components are harder, not easier. An Economics commentary of 800 words that must contain a diagram, named theory, application and evaluation leaves no room for an introduction that restates the article. A Theory of Knowledge exhibition commentary of a few hundred words per object has to establish the object, link it to the prompt and justify the link, which is three jobs in a paragraph. Practice at that compression is coachable and rarely coached.

Treat every figure below as a prompt to check rather than as gospel. The IB revises limits and subject guides between syllabus cycles, and the authoritative version is the current subject guide the school holds. What does not change is the principle: find the limit before planning, plan to it, and never write long with the intention of cutting.
