dubai/umm-suqeim.programmesIntro: Within a few streets of each other, Umm Suqeim households run children through four different assessment frameworks. The notes below describe each one from a parent's point of view: what the reporting actually tells you, and where it hides a problem.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Reported as subject grades out of 7 with three bonus points available from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. Predicted grades issued by the school drive university applications a full year before results exist.
programmes.countryNote: In an Umm Suqeim household with younger siblings, the Diploma is the programme that breaks the evening. The internally assessed components do not appear on a weekly homework diary, so the workload is invisible until a deadline is two weeks out. Households that survive it put the eldest's coursework block in the calendar at the start of the term rather than reacting to it.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria marked out of 8 and converted to a 1-7 grade. Reports arrive as criterion strands rather than percentages, which is more informative than a single mark and much harder for a parent to act on without the task-specific clarification the teacher used.
programmes.countryNote: The practical question for an Umm Suqeim family is the one that arrives at 16: stay in the IB continuum or move to an IGCSE school. The honest input is the Criterion C and D profile in Mathematics and the sciences, because those criteria sit closest to what Diploma Higher Level asks for. A strong overall MYP grade built on Criterion A alone is a weaker signal than it looks.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Terminal examinations in a June or November series, one syllabus at a time. Cambridge Mathematics is 0580 and Physics 0625; the Pearson Edexcel equivalents are 4MA1 and 4PH1. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, with Core carrying a lower grade ceiling than parents usually realise when the entry is made.
programmes.countryNote: Umm Suqeim children attend British-curriculum schools across Jumeirah, Al Safa and Al Barsha, and those schools do not all use the same board. In a two-child household it is common for siblings to hold entries with different boards for the same subject, which means two different paper structures and two different revision plans. Checking both statements of entry takes five minutes and prevents a term of wasted work.

programmes.name: Mandatory UAE subjects
programmes.ageRange: All year groups in Dubai private schools
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum. KHDA calculates instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit and advises a minimum lesson length of 25 minutes for any mandatory subject, with total weekly time the binding requirement rather than individual lesson length.
programmes.countryNote: Non-Arab households in Umm Suqeim meet Arabic as an additional language, taught in separate classes from Arabic as a first language because KHDA strictly prohibits combining the two groups. Support here is a different job from IB or IGCSE subject tuition: it is vocabulary, script fluency and the school's own assessment format, and it responds well to short frequent sessions rather than long weekly ones.

dubai/umm-suqeim.subjectsIntro: Requests from this district cluster around the sciences, mathematics and Arabic, with English literature appearing later in the Diploma. Each note below names what the component actually rewards, so a parent can tell whether tuition is the right purchase.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Higher Level carries a Paper 3 worth a fifth of the grade, built from extended multi-part problems. Students arriving from a strong IGCSE Extended background are fluent in method and short on written justification, which is where Paper 3 marks live. The exploration adds another fifth and is done entirely outside lessons.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Heavier on statistics and modelling, with calculator use assumed throughout. The failure pattern is answering with an output rather than an interpretation: a regression line with no sentence about what it means in context earns the calculation marks and loses the rest.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Two external papers plus a scientific investigation worth a fifth of the grade. Uncertainty handling and extended written explanation are the recurring weaknesses. Students who can derive an equation but not explain a field in words plateau in the middle bands however much content they revise.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics and organic mechanisms carry the Higher Level difficulty, and data-based questions reward a structured error analysis. The internally assessed investigation is marked on design and evaluation, so a neat experiment with a thin evaluation section caps out well below its apparent quality.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The content is large and the marks turn on command terms. Outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each expect a different answer shape and length. Revision by rereading produces students who know the material and under-write every six-mark question on the paper.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: A mandatory Dubai school subject for non-Arab students, taught in classes separate from Arabic as a first language. Progress depends on script fluency and high-frequency vocabulary far more than on grammar rules, and short frequent sessions beat one long weekly lesson for retention.

subjects.name: Islamic Education for non-Arabs
subjects.description: Delivered in the language of the school's licensed curriculum for non-Arab students under KHDA rules. Assessment is school-set, so support is built around the school's own scheme of work and vocabulary lists rather than around an external syllabus document.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen analysis under time pressure and separates grades more than any other component. Higher Level adds an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on a studied text. The Individual Oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue and broad enough to find in two texts.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three internally assessed commentaries on three articles from three different units, each within an 800-word limit. Higher Level adds a quantitative Paper 3 that students from a literary background underestimate. Accurate diagrams with labelled axes earn more than additional prose does.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended / Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The tier decision is the single most consequential entry choice at IGCSE, because Core and Foundation cap the achievable grade. It is usually made in Year 10 and can sometimes be amended, but only inside the board's entry window, which closes months before the papers.

subjects.name: Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0653 / 0654)
subjects.description: A compressed route through all three sciences for students with crowded option blocks. Everything is examinable and nothing is revisited, so a Year 10 gap stays a gap into Year 11. Worth confirming which award your child is entered for before planning any science tuition.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 / 0511)
subjects.description: A different syllabus from First Language English with its own mark scheme and the one most frequently mis-entered in a mid-year admission. The extended writing tasks have fixed word ranges and a required register, and register is where marks disappear rather than grammar.

dubai/umm-suqeim.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so geography does not restrict who is available. It does decide when an evening can start and whether two siblings can be booked back to back, which is the question this district actually asks.

regions.note: Inland from Kite Beach towards Al Wasl Road, with older villas alongside newer low-rise apartments. The mixed housing means mixed school routes: some children walk or are collected within minutes, others are on a 40-minute bus. A 16:15 start suits the first group and 17:00 the second.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim 2
regions.note: Almost entirely residential and quiet, between Al Manara and the beach. Households here are more often long-settled with two or three children, which is why consecutive sibling slots on one evening are the most common booking shape in this district.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim 3
regions.note: The stretch past Madinat Jumeirah towards Al Sufouh, with larger compounds and a higher proportion of shorter leases. Mid-year arrivals are more common here than anywhere else nearby, and those students need a diagnostic session before a teaching plan is worth writing.

regions.name: Al Manara
regions.note: Immediately inland across Al Wasl Road, with villa plots and longer bus routes to schools in Al Barsha and Al Safa. Children arrive home later than their coastal neighbours, so 17:00 is the realistic weekday start and weekend mornings are heavily requested.

regions.name: Jumeirah 3
regions.note: The next district north-east along Jumeirah Beach Road, feeding many of the same schools in Al Safa and Jumeirah 1. Shared bus routes mean arrival windows vary by fifteen minutes, so sessions are set at the later edge of the window rather than the earlier one.

regions.name: Al Safa and Al Wasl
regions.note: Inland, holding several of the secondary schools Umm Suqeim children attend. The Al Safa interchange in the late afternoon is the usual reason a fixed start time slips, which is an argument for a session that does not depend on anybody driving.

regions.name: Al Sufouh and Knowledge Village
regions.note: South-west along the coast, with a cluster of secondary schools and the university quarter. Older students here sometimes attend evening or weekend enrichment on campus, so tuition is scheduled around that rather than around the school day.

regions.name: Al Barsha
regions.note: A short drive inland and the destination for a large share of Umm Suqeim secondary commuters. Buses from Al Barsha arrive back late enough that a 16:00 session rarely works in term time; 17:15 is the practical floor for those households.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Dubai Hills
regions.note: Further inland, reached through the Al Khail Road corridor. Families who moved outward for space but kept a Jumeirah school place face the longest commute in this set, and they book weekend slots more often than weekday ones.

schoolClusters.city: Umm Suqeim and the Jumeirah coast
schoolClusters.note: The schools nearest Umm Suqeim run British and IB routes side by side, and some offer both at sixth form. Students supported through IB Gram attend schools in this cluster; naming them implies no relationship with any of them.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh, Al Barsha and the inland corridor
schoolClusters.note: Where most Umm Suqeim secondary commuters end up. Board choices differ school by school in this cluster, so a household with two children at two of these schools can be holding Cambridge entries for one and Pearson Edexcel for the other in the same subject.

schoolClusters.city: Arabian Ranches, Dubai Hills and Meadows
schoolClusters.note: The outward move many Umm Suqeim families make for space, usually keeping the same school for a year or two first. The commute is long enough that tuition shifts to weekends, and the handover year is when gaps appear in the child's weakest subject.

sections.heading: Four Umm Suqeim households and what each one actually buys
paragraphs: Tuition requests from this district fall into a small number of shapes, and the shape matters more than the subject. A household with three children at two schools has a scheduling problem that no amount of subject expertise solves. A household that arrived in October has a diagnostic problem. A household with one Year 13 candidate has a coursework problem that will consume the whole spring. Selling the same weekly hour to all three is why families end up disappointed with tuition in general.

The long-settled villa household is the most common here. Two or three children, often across primary and secondary, frequently at different schools because the sibling place did not come through or because one moved for a specific sixth form. What they need is a single committed evening with consecutive slots, and what breaks them is the arrival of the eldest's internally assessed coursework, which does not appear on any homework diary until it is nearly late.

The apartment household, concentrated in Umm Suqeim 1, is usually one or two children on a shorter lease with a higher chance of a mid-year arrival. Their first purchase should be diagnosis, not teaching. A student who was comfortably ahead in a national curriculum can be two years behind the written-explanation expectations of an IGCSE set while being ahead on content, and a general assessment will not reveal that. A syllabus-referenced baseline will.

The third shape is the household whose real gap is Arabic. It is mandatory, it is examined by the school, it occupies timetable time every week, and because it is nobody's priority it drifts for years and then becomes urgent in Year 9. The fourth is the single-candidate household in the final Diploma year, where the answer is almost always a short coursework block followed by weekly subject sessions, rather than four tutors booked at once in February.

sections.heading: The three Umm Suqeims, and why the school route is not the same
paragraphs: The numbering is not cosmetic. Umm Suqeim 1 sits closest to Jumeirah 2 and Al Safa, so its children are more often in the Jumeirah and Al Safa school cluster with short collections and a realistic 16:15 session start. Umm Suqeim 2 is deeper into the villa grid and quieter, with slightly longer runs to the same schools. Umm Suqeim 3 reaches towards Al Sufouh, which puts the Al Sufouh and Al Barsha schools within easier reach and often means a bus rather than a car.

Those differences translate directly into tuition logistics. A household whose children are home at 15:10 can run a 16:00 session with time to eat. A household on a bus route from Al Barsha is realistically looking at 17:15, because the bus does not arrive at a reliable time and a session that starts late ends late, which matters when a younger sibling is booked behind it. Setting the slot at the later edge of the arrival window costs fifteen minutes and saves a term of rescheduling.

There is a second-order effect worth naming. Because Umm Suqeim 3 households turn more often than the others, their children are more likely to have joined mid-year, and mid-year joiners are the group most likely to be in the wrong set or entered for the wrong syllabus. A child admitted in November into Year 11 may have been placed on the basis of their previous school's report rather than against the actual syllabus they are now sitting, and nobody has the time to check.

None of this restricts who is available, because lessons run over live video rather than by car. It determines the hour. The only local variable that genuinely matters once the tutor pool is national rather than drivable is when the child is in a chair, fed, and able to concentrate.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and the mandatory UAE subjects
paragraphs: Every Dubai private school teaches these alongside its licensed international curriculum. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. KHDA's own guidance states that these requirements must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 applying to schools whose year begins in April.

Two of KHDA's rules change how support should be arranged. The first is class organisation: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. The second is language of instruction: Standard Arabic is required as the main language for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

KHDA also sets the time arithmetic. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and it is advised that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. For the mandatory subjects, KHDA states that use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, which is the reason support here works from the school's own scheme and vocabulary lists rather than from an outside course.

KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That is a requirement on schools, not on private tutors, and IB Gram claims no standing with KHDA for itself or its tutors. What a tutor can do is work on script fluency, high-frequency vocabulary and the format of the school's own assessments, which is where most non-Arab students in Umm Suqeim lose marks.

sections.heading: Stacking siblings: two children, two curricula, one evening
paragraphs: A household with a Year 7 in the Middle Years Programme and a Year 11 sitting Cambridge IGCSE is running two unrelated systems from one kitchen table. The younger child is assessed against four criteria per subject with no external paper; the elder is heading for terminal examinations with entries already submitted. Both need help and the help has nothing in common, which is exactly why families try to solve it with one tutor and end up disappointed.

The arrangement that works is a single committed block with separate specialists inside it. The younger child takes the first slot, because attention at 16:00 is better than at 18:00. The elder takes the second, when a ninety-minute session on past papers is actually productive. One evening is lost rather than three, and both children see the household taking the work seriously, which is not a trivial effect in a family where one child is visibly in an exam year and the other is not.

The second problem is board mismatch between siblings. It is entirely normal in Umm Suqeim for two children at two schools to hold entries with different boards for the same subject, because schools choose independently and some split by department. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both IGCSE Mathematics and they tier, time and structure differently. A parent who buys revision resources once, for both children, has bought the wrong ones for one of them.

The third is the quiet unfairness of attention. In most multi-child households the exam-year child absorbs everything and the younger one coasts for two years, then arrives in Year 10 with gaps nobody noticed. Booking the younger child a shorter session in the same block is the cheapest insurance available against that, and it is far cheaper than the remediation it prevents.

sections.heading: What a term costs an Umm Suqeim household, in context
paragraphs: Market rates in Dubai are wide. One Dubai content provider advertises online tuition from AED 45 to AED 65 an hour and one platform from roughly AED 33; a Dubai agency publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; a Dubai cost survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 and specialist exam-year tuition at AED 200 to AED 450 and above; one premium provider publishes AED 650. Monthly packages seen in the market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are other people's published figures, named as such, not IB Gram's price list.

The useful question for a household is not the hourly rate but the termly total, because that is the number that competes with everything else in the budget. A single weekly session across a thirteen-week term is thirteen hours. Two children at one session each is twenty-six. A Diploma candidate on two sessions a week in the run-up to the papers is twenty-six by themselves. Multiplying the band by the term before committing is a five-minute exercise that prevents the far more common pattern of starting in October and stopping in January.

There is useful context from the regulator on the other side of the ledger. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there will be no increase in school fees for private schools in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. For a household already paying Dubai school fees for two or three children, a flat fee year is the difference between a tuition budget existing and not existing.

sections.heading: An online tutor against a tutor in the villa
paragraphs: This is a fair question in a district of large plots with quiet rooms, so it deserves the honest version. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai; that service exists only in India, and no tutor is sent to an Umm Suqeim address. The argument for online here is not primarily cost, although it usually is cheaper once travel is priced in. It is who you get to choose from.

A tutor who drives to Umm Suqeim 2 at 17:00 on a Wednesday is selected from the people who can be in Umm Suqeim 2 at 17:00 on a Wednesday. For Year 8 Mathematics that is a large group. For Chemistry at Higher Level under the current guide, for a Pearson Edexcel 4PH1 entry specifically, or for Arabic as an additional language at secondary level, it narrows sharply. Over live video the selection criterion becomes the syllabus rather than the postcode, and for a multi-child household it also means two specialists in one evening rather than two drivers.

Continuity is the second argument and it compounds over years rather than weeks. A travelling tutor loses sessions to traffic, to their own summer away, and to the end of a contract. An online slot survives a family trip, a Ramadan timetable change and a move from Umm Suqeim to Dubai Hills with no gap and no rematch. Across a two-year Diploma that reliability is worth more than any individual lesson.

The honest counter-case: very young children concentrate better with an adult physically present, practical laboratory technique cannot be taught through a screen, and a household with poor connectivity or no quiet room will find online harder. In a villa district with space, those apply less often than the price difference suggests, but when they apply they are decisive and should be acted on.

sections.heading: Who regulates your child's school, and what that means for a household that moves
paragraphs: Umm Suqeim families move within the UAE more often than they expect to, and the regulator changes with the emirate. In Dubai it is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain it is the Department of Education and Knowledge, which u.ae says supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools there. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages researched for this project, which is a strange gap given how many Dubai families eventually relocate to the capital.

Sharjah's Private Education Authority regulates private education in that emirate, Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge does the same there, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. The Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah authorities also approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum and fee approval, not only inspection, sits with the emirate regulator in those cases.

For a household considering a move, the practical consequences are inspection reports in a different format, a different fee-approval regime, and a different attestation route for certificates at the end. The curriculum itself does not change if the school holds the same licence, and a Cambridge or IB entry transfers with the student, but the paperwork and the published school information do change.

There is one rule worth knowing before any relocation to Abu Dhabi. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Treat that as press-reported and verify against the current ADEK policy document before relying on the exact wording.

sections.heading: The line a tutor cannot cross on internally assessed work
paragraphs: Every IB subject carries an internally assessed component worth a fifth or more of the grade, and in a household where both parents work the temptation to outsource it is real. One operation in this market sells finished Internal Assessments at a fixed price. Buying one is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence lands on the candidate, not the vendor.

What a tutor is permitted to do is substantial and worth paying for. Teaching the underlying content. Explaining what each lettered criterion asks for and how marks are allocated across them. Interrogating a proposed research question until it is narrow enough to answer. Pointing out that a planned method will not generate usable data before three weeks are spent on it. Reading the student's own draft and naming which criterion is not yet met. Teaching the referencing convention the school requires.

What a tutor must not do is author any part of the work, supply sentences for insertion, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, provide the data, or hand over a completed example as a template to adapt. The authenticity test is conversational: a supervisor asks the candidate to explain their own method and reasoning, and a student who cannot do that has a problem no document can fix.

In practice this is why coursework support here is sold as a block of sessions timed to the school's internal deadlines, with the student drafting between them. It is slower than the alternative and it is the only version that survives scrutiny. A provider offering anything faster is selling your child a risk they do not understand.

sections.heading: Starting, with more than one child in the house
paragraphs: Begin with documents rather than a conversation about tutors. For each child: the most recent school report, the latest marked assessment with the mark shown, and the subject list with syllabus codes. In a two-board household that third item is the one that changes the plan, because it tells you whether the two children can share any resource at all.

Then name one weakness per child rather than a subject. Help with Chemistry is hard to act on; help with mole calculations and the evaluation criterion of the investigation is a brief a tutor can start on in the first fifteen minutes. The narrower the request, the better the match and the more useful the trial.

Book the trial sessions in the block you intend to keep, not at a convenient one-off time. If Tuesday at 16:15 and 17:30 is the plan, test it. Half the reason tuition stops after two months in this district is that the slot was never realistic once the bus, the food and the younger child's bedtime were all accounted for.

Availability is finite and worth saying plainly. Higher Level sciences, Mathematics and Economics are requested in the same late-afternoon window across every Dubai district, and unusual combinations narrow the pool further. If nothing suitable is free at the hour you want, the options are a different weekday, a weekend morning, or a short wait. Seating a student with a tutor who does not know the syllabus to fill a slot is worse than waiting a fortnight, and you will be told which situation you are in.

process.title: Gather the paperwork for each child
process.description: The latest report, the most recent marked paper and the subject list with syllabus codes. In a household where two children attend two schools, the codes reveal whether they are on the same board, which decides whether any resource or revision plan can be shared between them.

process.title: Decide the household block, then the tutors
process.description: Pick the single evening and the two or three consecutive slots you can actually keep, allowing for the latest bus arrival rather than the earliest. Matching tutors into a realistic block works; matching tutors first and hoping the week absorbs them does not.

process.title: Name one weakness per child
process.description: A specific component, topic or criterion rather than a subject. This is what makes the trial session useful instead of diagnostic-by-accident, and it lets a tutor say honestly in the first session whether the problem is content, technique or timing.

process.title: Run the trials inside the real block
process.description: Test the slot as well as the tutor. If the younger child cannot concentrate at 16:15 after a 40-minute bus, that is better discovered in a trial than in week six, and the fix is usually fifteen minutes and a snack rather than a different tutor.

process.title: Review both children together each term
process.description: Compare each tutor's view against the school's own assessment data at the end of term. Disagreement between the two is the most useful signal a parent gets, and in a multi-child household it is also where a quietly coasting younger sibling first becomes visible.

whyPoints.title: Built for households, not just students
whyPoints.description: Consecutive sibling slots in one weekly block, separate specialists inside it, and one calendar commitment rather than three. For a villa household with children across primary and secondary, the scheduling is the problem tuition most often fails on.

whyPoints.title: Arabic treated as an examined subject
whyPoints.description: Arabic and Islamic Education are mandatory in Dubai private schools and carry real marks. Support works from the school's own scheme and vocabulary rather than an outside course, because KHDA prohibits additional content for these subjects without Ministry permission.

whyPoints.title: Both IGCSE boards, checked by code
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different courses with different tiers and papers. Matching begins from the code on each child's statement of entry, which in a two-school household is the only way to avoid buying the wrong revision plan for one of them.

whyPoints.title: Figures you can trace
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page is attributed to the provider or survey that published it, with the date. Nothing here is presented as IB Gram's own price, and a quote you receive should be weighed against those published bands.

whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no permit, accreditation or partnership with KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and has no Dubai premises. Named schools are context for curricula and commutes, not relationships.

whyPoints.title: A slot that survives the year
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means the same tutor through a summer abroad, a Ramadan timetable change and a move to another Dubai district. Continuity across a two-year programme does more for a grade than any single excellent lesson.

faqs.question: Can two of my children have tutoring on the same evening in Umm Suqeim?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the arrangement most households here end up with. Each child gets their own tutor and their own syllabus, booked back to back in one block so the family commits a single evening rather than three. Put the younger child first, because concentration at 16:15 is better than at 18:00, and give the older child the longer second slot when ninety minutes of past-paper work is actually productive. Consecutive booking does not reduce the hourly rate, but it removes the second and third car journeys and makes the commitment survivable across a whole term.

faqs.question: My child joined a Dubai school mid-year. What should we do first?
faqs.answer: Buy diagnosis before teaching. A student who arrives in October from a different system has been placed on the basis of their previous school's report rather than against the syllabus they are now sitting, and nobody at the school has time to check. Three sessions against the live syllabus document will show what is genuinely known, what is ahead, and what has never been met. Content is often ahead while written explanation and paper technique lag badly. A teaching plan written without that baseline usually spends six months reteaching what the child already holds.

faqs.question: Is Arabic really compulsory at my child's British curriculum school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and the federal position is that private schools must cover Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies whatever else they teach. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in these subjects, because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and combined classes are strictly prohibited. The lesson is on the timetable every week and the marks appear on reports, which is why a grade that has drifted since Year 4 tends to surface as a problem in Year 9.

faqs.question: What does Arabic tutoring for a non-Arab child actually work on?
faqs.answer: Script fluency first, then high-frequency vocabulary, then the format of the school's own assessments. Grammar rules matter less at this stage than being able to read and write the script at speed, because a student who decodes slowly runs out of time on every task regardless of what they know. KHDA states that using different or additional content for the mandatory subjects without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, so support is built from the school's own scheme of work and word lists. Short frequent sessions, two or three a week, retain far better than one long weekly lesson.

faqs.question: How much should we budget for a term of tutoring for two children?
faqs.answer: Work from hours, not from the hourly rate. One session a week each across a thirteen-week term is twenty-six hours. At the budget online bands published by Dubai providers, around AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, that is roughly AED 1,170 to AED 1,690. At the specialist bands reported by a Dubai cost survey, AED 200 to AED 450 and above, the same twenty-six hours is AED 5,200 to AED 11,700. Those are market figures from other providers, not IB Gram's prices. Do the termly arithmetic before the first session rather than after the fourth month.

faqs.question: Do my two children need different tutors if they study the same subject?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, for two reasons. Their schools may use different boards, and Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 tier, time and structure IGCSE Mathematics differently, so the paper technique diverges even though the mathematics does not. They are also at different stages with different weaknesses, and a tutor optimising for a Year 11 terminal paper teaches differently from one building Year 8 fluency. The exception is a short shared revision block on genuinely common content, which can work for siblings close in age at the same school on the same board.

faqs.question: Which schools do Umm Suqeim children commute to?
faqs.answer: Mostly schools in Umm Suqeim itself, Jumeirah, Al Safa, Al Sufouh and Al Barsha, with some households travelling as far as Arabian Ranches or Dubai Hills for a particular sixth form. Between them those schools run British routes to IGCSE and A Level, full IB continuum routes, and a few offering both at sixteen. Because the systems differ, the useful information for tuition is never the school name alone: it is the syllabus code on the statement of entry, which tells a tutor which papers your child will actually sit.

faqs.question: Why does my younger child's progress slip during the exam year of an older sibling?
faqs.answer: Because household attention is finite and visibly concentrated on the child with public examinations. The younger one coasts for eighteen months, nobody notices because no external grade is at stake, and the gap becomes visible in Year 10 when it is expensive to close. The cheapest insurance is a short regular session for the younger child inside the same weekly block, forty-five minutes rather than ninety, aimed at fluency rather than content. It costs a fraction of the remediation it prevents and it also stops the exam year dominating the household entirely.

faqs.question: Does ADEK or KHDA allow a school teacher to tutor my child privately?
faqs.answer: Not their own enrolled students. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Treat the ADEK wording as press-reported and check the current policy document before relying on it. The practical consequence is simple: asking for your child's own class teacher privately is the one request not to make, however convenient it appears.

faqs.question: What changes if we move from Dubai to Abu Dhabi or Sharjah?
faqs.answer: The regulator changes and with it the inspection format, the fee-approval regime and the attestation route. Dubai is overseen by KHDA; Abu Dhabi and Al Ain by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises licensing and accreditation there; Sharjah by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which also approves fees, curricula and assessment methods. Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. A Cambridge or IB entry transfers with the student; the paperwork around it does not.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our villa in Umm Suqeim?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are offered only in India. Sessions run one-to-one over live video at a fixed weekly slot. In a multi-child household that is usually the easier arrangement regardless of preference, because two children can see two different specialists in one evening without a second car journey. It also means the tutor is chosen for knowing your child's syllabus rather than for being able to reach Umm Suqeim 2 at five o'clock on a weekday.

faqs.question: Are Dubai school fees going up in 2026-27?
faqs.answer: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there will be no increase in school fees for private schools in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. For a household paying fees for two or three children, that flat year is often what makes a tuition budget possible at all. Dubai's sector is also expanding: seven new private schools are opening for 2026-27, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places after a 6 per cent rise in enrolment during 2025-26.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Middle Years Programme when there is no exam?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the work looks different from exam tuition. MYP subjects are assessed against four criteria marked out of 8, converted to a 1-7 grade, using task-specific clarifications the teacher writes. A tutor's job is to translate those criteria into what the student should actually produce, because a report showing Criterion A at 6 and Criterion D at 3 is telling you something precise that most parents cannot act on unaided. Criterion C and D performance in Mathematics and the sciences is also the best available predictor of how a student will cope with Diploma Higher Level.

faqs.question: How long before the May papers should a Diploma candidate start tutoring?
faqs.answer: If the problem is coursework, the autumn of the final year at the latest, because the exploration and Extended Essay deadlines sit months before the papers and cannot be recovered afterwards. If the problem is content, two terms gives time to rebuild; one term gives time to patch. If the problem is execution, which is timing, command terms and showing working, eight weeks of intensive timed practice is often enough and starting earlier adds little. Diagnosing which of the three you are dealing with takes one session with a past paper and a stopwatch.

faqs.question: What should we ask a tutor before booking a recurring slot?
faqs.answer: Four things. Which syllabus code have you taught, and when. What do you intend to fix first, in one sentence. What will my child do between sessions, and who marks it. And, for an individual tutor working privately in the UAE, do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. A tutor who cannot answer the second question specifically after a trial session has not diagnosed anything yet.

dubai/umm-suqeim.closingHeading: Start with the household, then the subject
dubai/umm-suqeim.closingBody: For most families in Umm Suqeim the first decision is not which tutor but which evening, and how many children are in it. Pick the block you can actually keep once the latest bus has arrived, gather the report, the marked paper and the syllabus codes for each child, and name one weakness each. Trials then run inside the real slot, so you test the logistics as well as the teaching. Lessons are one-to-one over live video; no tutor is sent to an Umm Suqeim address. Every AED figure on this page belongs to the published market and is attributed as such, and a rate for your household is quoted after the trial.

dubai/villanova.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover language courses by their actual course code and level, from Cambridge English as a Second Language through to Diploma Language B and ab initio, alongside the sciences and mathematics. A language tutor is matched to a syllabus, not to a mother tongue.

intro.heading: The language decisions nobody flags until it is too late
paragraphs: Villanova is a townhouse community off Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road, sitting between The Villa, Liwan and the Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City corridor. Its households are among the most linguistically mixed in the city: families where the parents share one language, the children answer in another, the school teaches in a third, and the state requires a fourth. That is an ordinary Dubai arrangement and it has specific academic consequences that almost nothing published about tutoring addresses.

The consequences arrive through entry decisions, and they are made early and quietly. A school chooses, usually in Year 9, whether a child is entered for Cambridge First Language English or for English as a Second Language. That choice is sensible on the day it is taken and it travels with the child: some university and sixth-form routes treat the two differently, and a student who could have managed the first-language paper with support is sometimes placed in the second-language one because it was the safer administrative option. Nobody revisits it in Year 11, by which point it is fixed.

A second decision sits on top. Dubai requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in every private school regardless of its licensed curriculum, and KHDA sets detailed rules about who takes which version and in which language it is taught. Families routinely treat these as non-subjects, discover a weak Arabic grade on a report card, and only then learn that the stream their child is in, Arabic as a first language or as an additional language, was itself a decision with its own consequences.

A third arrives at sixteen. The Diploma offers three broad language routes: Language A for students studying their strongest language as a literature or language-and-literature subject, Language B for competent second-language users, and ab initio for near-beginners. Choosing the wrong one is the single most common Diploma mis-selection in multilingual households, and it is not always obvious which way the error runs. A fluent speaker who cannot write analytically in that language can be wrongly placed in Language A; a student with strong grammar and no reading history can be wrongly placed in a course that will not stretch them.

IB Gram is a tutor-matching platform, not a school or a centre, with no premises in Dubai. For UAE families every lesson runs one to one over live video with a shared whiteboard and a recording the student keeps. We do not send a tutor to any UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India. For language tutoring that format matters more than for most subjects, because the specialist pool for a particular course, Arabic B at Higher Level or Spanish ab initio for instance, is small everywhere and would be vanishingly small if restricted to people willing to drive to Dubailand.

dubai/villanova.programmesIntro: Villanova children reach four routes, and the language component of each is the part this page treats in detail because it is the part least explained elsewhere.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11. For a multilingual household the language entries carry the most long-term weight: First Language English, English as a Second Language, English Literature, and a first or additional language entry in the family's own language where the school offers it. Cambridge tiers several non-language subjects into Core and Extended, with Core capping at grade C.
programmes.countryNote: GEMS FirstPoint School in neighbouring The Villa and the British-curriculum schools around Academic City and Dubai Silicon Oasis take most Villanova students on this route. The practical point is to ask the school, in Year 9, which English entry is planned and why, and to ask whether a first-language entry in the child's home language is available, because it is a genuine qualification and often goes unclaimed.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, including one from Studies in Language and Literature and one from Language Acquisition. That structure means every Diploma student takes two languages, which is why language placement matters more here than in any other qualification. Each subject also carries an internal assessment worth roughly a fifth to a quarter of the grade.
programmes.countryNote: Multilingual Villanova students often have the option of a bilingual diploma, awarded where a student completes two Language A subjects or a Language A plus a subject studied in that language. It is worth asking about explicitly, because it is a real distinction, it is frequently available to students who do not realise it, and nobody will suggest it unprompted.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria marked 0 to 8, including Language and Literature and Language Acquisition as separate groups. The criteria assess communication and comprehension explicitly, which exposes a gap between conversational fluency and academic register faster than a British curriculum does.
programmes.countryNote: This is where a multilingual child's profile becomes legible. A student who speaks a language at home but has never read in it will score well on oral criteria and poorly on written ones, and the Middle Years marks make that split visible. Three or four sessions on academic register in the weaker language is high-value work at this stage, before any Diploma course is chosen.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led units with descriptive reporting and no external examinations before the Year 6 Exhibition. For multilingual families the question at this stage is whether the home language is developing alongside the school language or being displaced by it, which the school's reporting will not tell you.
programmes.countryNote: The cheap and useful intervention here is reading in the home language, which costs nothing and preserves options later: a child who can read in their home language at eleven has a realistic Language A or first-language IGCSE route at fourteen, and a child who cannot does not. Families often realise this three years too late.

dubai/villanova.subjectsIntro: The list is weighted towards languages because that is where Villanova households most often need specialist help, with the sciences and mathematics included because they are the other half of most requests.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is an unseen guided analysis under timed conditions and the Individual Oral is internally assessed against a global issue the student selects. Students with strong spoken English and limited reading history can analyse a text and struggle to structure an argument in seventy-five minutes.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Assessed on receptive, productive and interactive skills rather than literary analysis. The recurring mark-loser is register: a student writes a blog in the tone of an essay, or a formal letter in the tone of a message, and loses marks that have nothing to do with their vocabulary.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: For students whose strongest language is Arabic. The demand is literary and analytical in Modern Standard Arabic, which is a different register from spoken dialect, and this gap accounts for most of the difficulty even among confident speakers.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: For competent second-language users. Script fluency under time, and the distance between dialect and Modern Standard Arabic, are the two places marks disappear. Short, frequent practice outperforms long grammar sessions by a wide margin.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: For near-beginners, with a prescribed set of themes and tightly defined assessment. It rewards systematic coverage rather than flair, which makes it unusually coachable; the common error is a student being placed here when they are already past the course's ceiling.

subjects.name: French B and Spanish B
subjects.description: Productive skills decide the grade: the written task and the individual oral. Students who have read widely still lose marks for failing to address every element of a prompt, which is a planning habit rather than a language limitation.

subjects.name: IGCSE First Language English
subjects.description: Reading and writing papers where evidence selection and timed planning separate grades. Students paraphrase the passage instead of selecting from it, which caps marks regardless of how fluent the writing is.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
subjects.description: More procedural than the first-language paper and frequently the right entry in multilingual households. Marks turn on following the directed-writing instruction exactly, with register and audience explicitly assessed, which makes it quick to improve with targeted work.

subjects.name: IGCSE Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: A genuine qualification that often goes unclaimed by families who assume their child's Arabic is only a school requirement. Where the school offers the entry, it is worth asking about, because it converts an existing strength into a certificated subject.

subjects.name: IGCSE English Literature
subjects.description: Textual detail is the currency. A student who has read the set text without annotating it writes general essays that settle in the middle bands, and no amount of tutoring substitutes for the reading itself.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 1 without a calculator exposes algebraic weakness a graphing display was hiding, and Higher Level adds proof by induction and complex numbers. Marks go missing on unjustified steps rather than wrong answers.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms dominate lost marks. For students working in a second language, the command terms are an additional hurdle: the chemistry is understood and the verb asked for is not delivered.

sections.heading: Who lives in Villanova, and what the language mix changes
paragraphs: Searching for IB and IGCSE tutors in Villanova produces the same generic results as searching for any Dubai community, which misses what is distinctive about this one. Villanova and the communities immediately around it, The Villa, Liwan and the Silicon Oasis corridor, hold a high proportion of households where more than two languages are in daily use. The parents may share Arabic, Hindi, Urdu, Tagalog, Russian or Arabic dialect; the children often answer in English; the school teaches in English; and the emirate requires Arabic alongside whatever else is on the timetable.

That arrangement is completely normal and it produces a specific academic profile. These students are usually strong communicators and frequently weaker at academic register in every language they speak, including the one they are most fluent in. A child can hold a confident conversation in English and be unable to write a formal analytical paragraph in it; the same child can speak excellent Arabic at home and be unable to write Modern Standard Arabic to an examined standard. Neither is a deficiency. Both are predictable and both are coachable, but only if named correctly.

The practical consequence is that the entry decisions matter more here than the teaching does. Which English paper the child is entered for, which Arabic stream they sit, and which Diploma language courses they take will shape their results more than any individual tutor will. Those decisions are made by schools, usually sensibly, usually administratively, and usually without a conversation that weighs the long-term options against the short-term safety of the choice.

The table below maps common household language profiles against the entries worth asking the school about. It is a prompt for a conversation rather than a prescription, because the right answer depends on a piece of the student's own writing rather than on their passport.

sections.heading: First Language English or English as a Second Language
paragraphs: This is the entry decision with the longest shadow, and it is usually taken in Year 9 on the basis of a school's internal assessment. Both qualifications are legitimate and both are widely accepted. They are not interchangeable, and the difference is worth understanding before the decision is locked rather than after the certificate arrives.

Cambridge First Language English, syllabus 0500, assesses reading and writing at the level expected of a strong first-language user. Evidence selection, timed planning and controlled register decide grades, and the most common failure is paraphrasing a passage rather than selecting from it. It is the harder paper and it sits more naturally alongside English Literature.

Cambridge English as a Second Language, syllabuses 0510 and 0511, assesses functional competence across reading, writing, listening and speaking. It is more procedural, which makes it faster to improve with targeted work, and for a student who arrived in English-medium education recently it is the honest and correct entry. The directed-writing question in particular rewards following the instruction exactly, including register and audience, which is a teachable skill rather than a matter of fluency.

The risk is a student placed in the second-language entry who could have handled the first-language one with two terms of support. That happens because the second-language route is the safer administrative choice and nobody is accountable for the counterfactual. The way to test it is evidence: a timed first-language-style response, marked against the 0500 criteria, early in Year 9. If it lands credibly, the conversation with the school is worth having while there is still time.

sections.heading: The KHDA rules on Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies
paragraphs: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's mandatory-subjects requirements had to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For a Villanova family this is not a footnote: these subjects occupy timetable hours, appear on the report card and have their own organisational rules that most parents have never read.

The class organisation rule is explicit. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. That means the stream your child sits is a real distinction with different content, not an administrative label.

The language-of-instruction rules follow from it. KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students. For non-Arabs, Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes.

Two further points matter for tutoring specifically. For these subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, so support here means working through the school's own material rather than introducing a parallel course. And schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a concrete and checkable thing to ask your school about.

sections.heading: Diploma language courses: A, B and ab initio
paragraphs: Every Diploma student takes two languages, one from Studies in Language and Literature and one from Language Acquisition. In a multilingual household that creates both an opportunity and a trap, and schools tend to default to the arrangement that is easiest to timetable rather than the one that is best for the student.

Language A treats the language as a literary and analytical subject. It is the right route for a student whose strongest language it is, and it demands reading history and the ability to write analytically in that language. Fluent speech is not sufficient: a student who speaks a language at home and has never read a novel in it will struggle in Language A, and that is the most common mis-placement in this direction.

Language B is for competent second-language users and is assessed on receptive, productive and interactive skills rather than literary analysis. Register is where the marks go: writing a blog in the tone of an essay loses marks that have nothing to do with vocabulary. Ab initio is for near-beginners, with prescribed themes and tightly defined assessment, which makes it unusually coachable. The error in this direction is a student placed in ab initio who is already beyond its ceiling and ends the course bored and under-credited.

The option worth raising explicitly is the bilingual diploma, awarded where a student completes two Language A subjects, or a Language A plus a subject studied in that language. Many Villanova students qualify or could qualify with modest adjustment, and almost none are told. Where a school does not teach the home language, a school-supported self-taught Language A route may be possible at Standard Level; ask the Diploma coordinator rather than assuming it is unavailable.

sections.heading: What language tutoring costs, and why the pool is small
paragraphs: Market rates in Dubai, read in October 2026 from providers' own published pages and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, put a qualified subject tutor working online at AED 150 to AED 300 an hour and an IB or IGCSE specialist at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. In-home visits run AED 180 to AED 500 with travel priced in. Budget platforms advertise from AED 33 to AED 65. Those are market figures, not an IB Gram price list.

Language courses sit at the specialist end of that range for a structural reason rather than a commercial one. The pool of tutors who have actually taught Arabic B at Higher Level, or Spanish ab initio, or Cambridge 0508 Arabic as a First Language, is small in absolute terms. A tutor who speaks the language fluently is not the same thing as a tutor who has taught that course and knows how its criteria award marks, and the difference shows up immediately in the first marked piece.

This is where the online format does its real work in Villanova. Restricting a Higher Level Arabic B search to tutors willing to drive to Dubailand on a weekday evening would reduce the available pool to almost nothing. Delivering over live video means the constraint is the tutor's experience of the course rather than their postcode, and for a scarce course that is the difference between a specialist and a fluent generalist.

Set the rate against the rest of the education bill. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year under Dubai's second economic incentives package, valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Fees are the fixed part of this year's cost; tutoring is the variable part, and in a multilingual household the highest-value spend is often one entry-decision consultation rather than a year of weekly lessons.

sections.heading: Where marks actually go in a language paper
paragraphs: Language marks are lost in a small number of predictable places, and almost none of them are vocabulary. Parents assume the problem is words the student does not know. Examiners award marks for things the student did not do, which is a different category of problem and a far more fixable one.

The first is register. Every productive task names an audience and a text type, and the marks for register are allocated whether or not the student noticed. A formal email written in a conversational tone, or a blog written like an examination essay, loses those marks with perfect grammar. Teaching register is a matter of showing a student four model text types and having them produce each one twice.

The second is incomplete coverage of a prompt. Prompts usually contain two or three elements, and a student who answers the interesting one thoroughly and skips the others caps their own mark. This is a planning habit: thirty seconds spent numbering the elements of the prompt before writing recovers marks that no amount of fluency will.

The third is timed planning, and the fourth, in unseen analysis papers, is commentary that describes rather than analyses. A student who tells the examiner what a text says has written a summary; a student who explains how the text produces an effect has written an analysis. The distinction is teachable in a handful of sessions and is worth more than a term of vocabulary work. For students writing in a second language across the sciences too, the same pattern appears as command-term failure: the chemistry is understood and the verb asked for is not delivered.
bullets: Register: marks allocated for audience and text type, whether or not the student noticed
Prompt coverage: number the elements before writing, every time
Timed planning: a plan practised under time, not a plan in principle
Analysis not description: explain how the text works, not what it says

sections.heading: Translation tools, academic honesty and what counts as the student's own work
paragraphs: Multilingual households have a particular version of the academic honesty question, and it deserves a straight answer. A student who drafts in one language and translates into another, or who uses a translation tool to check a phrase, is doing something that sits somewhere on a spectrum, and the boundary is not always obvious even to a conscientious family.

The principle that resolves most cases is authorship. Work submitted for assessment must be the student's own, produced by them, representing their own competence in the language being assessed. A dictionary and, where the school permits it, a bilingual glossary are tools. A translation engine that produces the submitted text is not a tool but a substitute author, and in a language assessment it substitutes for exactly the thing being measured.

The same principle governs what a tutor may do. A tutor may teach register, show model text types, explain each assessment criterion in its own language, read a draft the student has written and name which criterion is underserved, and drill the structures the task needs. A tutor may not supply sentences for inclusion, rewrite a draft, translate the student's work into the target language, or produce any part of a submission. Feedback names the problem; authorship solves it for them.

Families should also know that boards hold copyright in syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables, which should be referenced and linked rather than redistributed. And one provider in this market sells completed Internal Assessments outright. Buying one creates an expulsion risk for the student, who is the person signing the authenticity declaration, not for the seller.
bullets: Submitted work must represent the student's own competence in the assessed language
Dictionaries and permitted glossaries are tools; a translation engine producing the text is not
A tutor may teach, model and give feedback; a tutor may not translate or supply text
Board materials are referenced and linked, never redistributed

sections.heading: Universities on the doorstep, and what they actually ask for
paragraphs: Dubai Academic City sits a short drive from Villanova, which makes the university conversation unusually concrete for families here. The campuses are visible, open evenings are easy to attend, and students meet undergraduates from their own schools. That proximity is an advantage, and it comes with a specific risk: assuming that because a university is nearby, its requirements are known.

They are not, and they vary. Mathematics route is the clearest example. The Diploma offers Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation, and some degree programmes specify one rather than the other, particularly in engineering, economics and the physical sciences. The only reliable source is the admissions page of the specific institution and programme, checked in the year of application. A tutoring page is not a source for that, and this one is not pretending to be.

The second layer is UAE Ministry of Education equivalency, which converts a school-leaving certificate into something a UAE institution or employer accepts. For the British track the sourced requirements are five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. For the American track, English proficiency requires IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying.

For the Diploma there is no published points threshold in that sourced guidance, so no number should be taken from any tutoring page, including this one. Check moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation authority directly. Equivalency is a regulatory process that no tutoring provider performs, guarantees or accelerates, and tutoring is not a requirement for it.

sections.heading: Availability, scheduling and the legal position
paragraphs: Villanova has a scheduling advantage over most of Dubailand. GEMS FirstPoint School sits in neighbouring The Villa and the Silicon Oasis corridor is short and reliable, so many families here have school runs measured in minutes rather than in the forty to seventy minutes typical of the Al Qudra communities. That means a 17:00 session is genuinely available, and three short language sessions a week are schedulable in a way they would not be further out.

Availability by course is the real constraint rather than time. Deep pools: IGCSE English as a Second Language, First Language English, the separate sciences, mathematics. Thin pools: Arabic as a First Language 0508, Diploma Arabic B at Higher Level, ab initio courses in any language, Higher Level Physics, Higher Level Economics. When a specialist in a scarce course is not free for a requested slot, the honest options are a different time with the right tutor, a short block with a related-course specialist to establish exactly what is needed, or a wait with a stated date.

On legality, individuals providing private tuition in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule, so any quoted figure is unverified.

One final clarification, because the claim is common in this market. A KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific licence for training institutes with premises in Dubai, renewed annually with the request made at least thirty days before expiry. IB Gram has no Dubai premises and holds no such permit, and no provider should be described as carrying regulator endorsement it does not hold.

process.title: Tell us the language entries, not just the subjects
process.description: Name the school, the year group, and which English entry, Arabic stream and Diploma language courses your child is on or heading towards. Those three facts shape the plan more than any subject list, and most families have never been asked for them by a tutoring provider.

process.title: Get evidence before any entry is locked
process.description: Where an entry decision is still open, the first session produces evidence rather than advice: a timed written response marked against the actual criteria and a short spoken assessment. The output is a written position you can take to the school, which is a different object from a tutor's opinion.

process.title: Match the course, not the mother tongue
process.description: A fluent speaker is not automatically a tutor for that language's examined course. We match on experience of the specific syllabus, including Cambridge 0508, Diploma Arabic B at Higher Level or ab initio, because the criteria decide the marks and fluency alone does not.

process.title: Run language work short and often
process.description: Three sessions of thirty to forty minutes a week, one skill each, with a short written piece produced between every pair. Villanova's short school runs make that schedulable. Productive language skills respond to frequency, which is why a single ninety-minute block underperforms.

process.title: Review on marked work, every six to eight weeks
process.description: Progress is measured on register, prompt coverage and timed planning in marked pieces, not on how the sessions felt. A free trial session is available before any commitment, with the length and conditions stated at booking, and it is best spent on a marked piece of real work.

whyPoints.title: Entry decisions treated as decisions
whyPoints.description: Which English paper, which Arabic stream and which Diploma language course a student sits will shape their results more than any individual tutor. We produce evidence on those questions rather than teaching around a placement nobody has examined.

whyPoints.title: Matched by syllabus, including the scarce ones
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0508 Arabic as a First Language, Diploma Arabic B at Higher Level and ab initio courses have thin specialist pools. We match on experience of the course criteria, not on fluency, because the two are different things and the first marked piece shows which you have.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery, which is what makes scarce courses possible
whyPoints.description: Every UAE lesson runs one to one over live video with a shared whiteboard and a recording kept. IB Gram does not operate home visits in Dubai; that service exists only in India. For a scarce language course, postcode-based matching would leave almost no pool at all.

whyPoints.description: The mandatory-subject requirements, the separate-class rule, the language-of-instruction rules and the forty-minute lesson unit are all stated here from KHDA's own guidelines. No competitor page in this market covers the Arabic requirement at all.
