sections.heading: Ramadan, the UAE academic calendar and when revision really happens
paragraphs: A revision plan drawn up without the UAE calendar in front of it will be wrong twice. School terms, public holidays and Ramadan all move the available hours, and Ramadan moves them most. School days shorten, afternoons become the least productive part of the day, and the hours after Iftar become the ones in which real work gets done. A student trying to hold a 4pm session through Ramadan is working at the worst time available to them.

The useful response is to change the shape of the week rather than abandon it. Shorter sessions, placed after Iftar, held slightly more often, keep momentum without asking a fasting student to concentrate during the hardest part of the day. Content that needs sustained abstraction, such as new calculus or a Higher Level mechanics topic, is better moved out of that period altogether, with consolidation and past-paper review taking its place.

The surrounding calendar matters too. Eid holidays, the long summer break and the winter break each sit at a different point relative to exam series, and a British-curriculum Year 11 facing a May or June series has a very different final stretch from a student entered for a November Edexcel sitting. Mapping the series against the school calendar is a one-page exercise that prevents a revision block landing in a week nobody is home.

Al Faseel families with an early start to the academic year should also check their own school's dates rather than assuming the regional norm, because start dates and therefore internal deadline cycles vary between schools in the same emirate.

sections.heading: Five questions worth asking before the first paid session
paragraphs: Most tutoring arrangements that fail do so for reasons visible in the first conversation. The questions below are the ones that surface them. They apply to any provider, including this one, and a tutor who cannot answer them comfortably is unlikely to be the specialist the student needs.

Start with the syllabus. Which board, which code, which tier? A tutor who says they teach IGCSE Chemistry without asking whether that is Cambridge 0620 or Pearson 4CH1 has not yet begun to match. Then ask about assessment: can they talk through the Internal Assessment criteria by letter, with the mark allocations, or do they describe it in general terms? The second answer predicts a session that teaches content and leaves the marks on the table.

The third question is about permits. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation free of charge for two years. Ask to see it. The fourth is about the academic-honesty boundary: what will they do with a draft Internal Assessment? Anything that sounds like producing the work rather than responding to it should end the conversation.

The fifth question is the dull one that matters most. What happens if this is not working in three weeks? A provider with a clear answer, including replacing the tutor rather than renegotiating, is describing a process. A provider who treats the question as a lack of confidence is describing a sales pitch.
bullets: Which board, which syllabus code, which tier?
Can you explain the assessment criteria by letter with mark allocations?
May I see your MoHRE private tuition work permit?
What exactly will you do, and not do, with a draft Internal Assessment?
What happens if this is not working in three weeks?

process.title: Map the week before picking a slot
process.description: Write out the five school days, mark what is genuinely fixed, and choose the hour that survives the worst week rather than the best one. For most Al Faseel families that is after 6pm, and after Iftar during Ramadan. A slot chosen this way lasts a term.

process.title: Name the board, the code and the tier
process.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both IGCSE Mathematics and they are different papers. Ask the exams officer for the exact codes and tiers and pass them on, so the proposed specialist is matched to the specification rather than the subject.

process.title: Send one recent marked assessment
process.description: A marked paper shows why a grade is where it is, which a report cannot. One recent assessment with the marker's comments gives a tutor more to work with than a long conversation, and it is what the free trial lesson is built around.

process.title: Take the trial lesson and read the diagnosis
process.description: The first session costs nothing and works on something the student has actually been set. It ends with a short written diagnosis naming the specific gaps and a recommended number of sessions, which is sometimes four rather than forty.

process.title: Review against the mandatory-subject load too
process.description: Each half term we check progress against the starting point and against total workload, including Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies. If the plan is overbooked, the right adjustment is usually fewer subjects supported properly, not more hours.

whyPoints.title: The slot comes first
whyPoints.description: Because lessons are taught online over live video, the session can sit in whatever hour an Al Faseel week leaves free, including after Iftar. Nobody has to be driving at that time, so the awkward but reliable slot is as easy to book as the convenient one.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the specification
whyPoints.description: A tutor is proposed against the exact board, syllabus code and tier your child's school entered, including Cambridge Core and Extended where they differ. Past-paper practice then matches the paper the student will actually sit.

whyPoints.title: The mandatory subjects are taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are examined subjects with their own homework and reports, taught under rules that prohibit substituting content without Ministry permission. Study plans here account for them instead of pretending the international curriculum is the whole week.

whyPoints.title: Honest boundaries on coursework
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches assessment criteria, questions method and responds to the student's own draft. No Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or Theory of Knowledge essay is produced for a student, and that boundary is stated at the start of any coursework block.

whyPoints.title: Figures are sourced or absent
whyPoints.description: Dirham amounts on this page are market rates published by UAE providers and rate trackers, read October 2026. Regulatory statements come from u.ae, the Dubai regulator's own guidelines, MoHRE and the exam boards. Anything that could not be verified is left out rather than estimated.

whyPoints.title: A planned end point
whyPoints.description: Sessions are reviewed each half term against the grade the student started at, and a plan that has done its work is stopped. Open-ended bookings that nobody revisits until results day are the most common waste in this market.

faqs.question: We live five minutes from school in Al Faseel. Why would we choose online lessons?
faqs.answer: Because proximity is not the binding constraint in a Fujairah City week. The free hours in an Al Faseel household tend to be late, after sport and prayers and often after Iftar, and the pool of people in this emirate who teach a particular Higher Level subject and are free at 8.45pm is very small. Online delivery lets the subject specialist be chosen on expertise and the time be chosen on your diary. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; lessons are taught live online, one to one, with the first one free.

faqs.question: How do we fit a weekly session around corniche sports and prayer times?
faqs.answer: Pick the hour that survives your worst week rather than your best one. Write out the five school days, mark what is genuinely fixed, and look at what is left; most Al Faseel families find one strong window after 6pm and one fragile one. Choose the strong one even if it is less convenient, because the fragile slot is what turns a weekly session into a fortnightly one. During Ramadan, move to a shorter session after Iftar rather than trying to hold an afternoon slot.

faqs.question: Does my child still have to take Arabic and Islamic Education in a British-curriculum school?
faqs.answer: Yes. The federal rule is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So a British-curriculum school in Fujairah timetables these subjects alongside IGCSE options, with their own homework, assessments and report entries. For planning purposes they are a real part of the workload competing for the same evening hours, which is why a study plan built only around IGCSE subjects tends to be overbooked from the start.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach my child a different Islamic Education syllabus if they are struggling?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody honest should offer to. The published guidance for mandatory UAE subjects states that the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. Support work therefore means teaching the prescribed content properly, improving comprehension, written structure and recall within it. For non-Arab students the subject is taught in the school's licensed curriculum language, and for Arab students in Standard Arabic, so the right support also matches the stream the school has placed the child in.

faqs.question: Why are Arabic classes split between Arab and non-Arab students?
faqs.answer: Because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ between the two groups. The published guidance requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language. Tutoring support should follow the same split, because material written for one stream is the wrong material for the other.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Core and Extended, and does it limit my child's grade?
faqs.answer: Yes, it limits it directly. Cambridge splits several IGCSE subjects into Core and Extended tiers, and the Core tier caps the grade available however well a student performs. Extended covers the core content plus the extended supplement and uses a different paper set. The tier should be decided on evidence from Year 10 assessments, and it has to be settled before the entry deadline, which sits months before the exam. If your child's marks do not match their effort, ask the exams officer which tier they were entered for.

faqs.question: When do Pearson Edexcel International GCSE results actually arrive?
faqs.answer: On published dates. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. The January date is the one to check if you are considering a November entry as a retake, because it decides whether a result exists in time for a given application deadline. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so plan from the live official timetable.

faqs.question: Is a Fujairah City tuition centre better value than one-to-one lessons?
faqs.answer: For a different problem, yes. A centre running a broad revision course gives structure across several subjects at a lower cost per hour, which suits a student who has fallen behind generally. It cannot work on one student's specific weakness in one paper of one syllabus, because the class is pitched at the median student. It also adds a journey to a week that may not have room for one and fixes the time to the centre's timetable. Match the format to the problem rather than to the headline rate.

faqs.question: What does tutoring cost compared with everything else we pay for school?
faqs.answer: School fees dominate, and a weekly session is a small share of annual education spend but a large share of the discretionary part. Rate trackers read in October 2026 put monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions at roughly AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Those are market figures, not our prices. The number that moves the total most is how long support runs, not the hourly rate.

faqs.question: How should we change the plan during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Shorten the sessions, move them after Iftar, and hold them slightly more often. Afternoons are the least productive hours for a fasting student, so a 4pm session is working against the day rather than with it. It also helps to move new abstract content, such as a fresh calculus topic or Higher Level mechanics, out of that window and use the period for consolidation and past-paper review instead. The pattern can switch back once the term calendar returns to normal.

faqs.question: Which board does my child's school use, and why does it matter so much?
faqs.answer: Ask the exams officer, because it changes what a session should contain. Cambridge identifies syllabuses by four-digit code such as 0580, 0620 and 0610; Pearson Edexcel uses codes such as 4MA1 and 4PH1. The two boards structure papers differently, assess practical skills differently and tier subjects differently. A student who practises the wrong board's past papers loses marks on question format rather than knowledge, which is the most avoidable loss available. Match the tutor to the code, not to the subject name.

faqs.question: Can split short sessions work better than one long evening?
faqs.answer: For some subjects, clearly. Arabic as an additional language, vocabulary-heavy humanities and anything that depends on retention respond better to two thirty or forty-minute sessions than to one long block, because frequency drives recall. Shorter sessions also survive a Fujairah City week better, since a forty-minute gap left by a cancelled activity is usable where ninety minutes is not. Longer blocks still suit coursework work and Higher Level problem-solving, where the student needs time to get into a hard question.

faqs.question: What should I ask a tutor before paying for the first session?
faqs.answer: Five things. Which board, code and tier do they teach? Can they explain the assessment criteria by letter with the mark allocations? May you see their MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is issued free of charge for two years under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023? Exactly what will they do, and refuse to do, with a draft Internal Assessment? And what happens if it is not working in three weeks? A provider with clear answers is describing a process rather than a pitch.

faqs.question: My child is in the Middle Years Programme. Should we wait until the Diploma to start?
faqs.answer: Usually no, because the habit that costs marks in the Diploma forms in the Middle Years Programme. Criterion-based assessment rewards investigation, communication and reflection, so a student can know the content well and still sit at a middling criterion level because the explanation of method is thin. That same weakness reappears in Diploma internal assessment, where it costs more. Working on how method and evaluation are written, using the school's own criterion feedback, is a better use of Middle Years sessions than content revision.

faqs.question: How quickly can a specialist be matched for a narrow Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: For common subjects, within a few days. For a narrow Higher Level course taken by very few students in this emirate, it can take a week or more to find a specialist free in the specific evening slot an Al Faseel family needs. The honest answer in that case is a timeline and alternative slot options rather than a nearest-available substitute who has not taught the course. If a match turns out wrong after two or three sessions, the tutor is changed rather than defended.

fujairah/al-faseel.closingBody: Send the subject, the board, the syllabus code, the tier where one applies, and one recent piece of marked work. Tell us the hour that survives your worst week rather than your best one, including a post-Iftar slot if that is the honest answer during Ramadan. We will propose a specialist matched to that exact specification, and the first lesson is free, taught online one to one over live video. It ends with a short written diagnosis naming the specific gaps and how many sessions they are likely to need, counted against the full workload your child is carrying rather than the international curriculum alone.

fujairah/al-gurfa.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the IB Diploma and Middle Years Programme, Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE, and the transition points between curricula. Each takes one student at a time and starts from where the student actually is rather than from where their year group should be.

intro.heading: Al Gurfa is several different households, and they need different advice
paragraphs: Al Gurfa sits on the coast south of Fujairah City, within reach of the city's schools and the port that gives much of this coast its economy. A tutoring enquiry from this district can come from very different places. One household has lived here for two generations, the children attend the same school their cousins did, and the question is about Arabic as a first language and a Diploma subject choice. Another arrived eight weeks ago on a three-year contract and has a Year 10 child who has never seen an IGCSE paper.

Those two families have almost nothing useful in common. The settled household is making a long decision: which post-16 route, which maths course, what a UAE university will expect in four years. The newly arrived household is managing an emergency: a curriculum change mid-course, a syllabus the student has not been taught, and an exam entry deadline that may already be close. Generic tutoring advice serves neither of them, which is why most pages in this market serve nobody.

A third pattern is specific to this coast. Fujairah's port, industrial and shipping sectors bring households on fixed-term postings, sometimes with one parent working offshore or on rotation. Schooling decisions in those households are made under a constraint nobody talks about: the family may not be here when the student sits the exams, so portability of qualification matters more than local convenience, and a curriculum that travels is worth more than one that does not.

A fourth is the household where the international curriculum and the home language pull in different directions. A student who speaks Arabic at home but studies in English faces a different workload from one whose home language is the school language, and the Arabic stream a school places them in has consequences that reach as far as Ministry of Education equivalency. That decision is often made administratively in Year 7 and never revisited.

What all four need is the same thing delivered differently: a specialist matched to the actual subject and the actual decision. IB Gram teaches UAE students online, one to one, over live video, and does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE. In an emirate with small school cohorts, that is what makes a match to a specific syllabus possible, rather than a match to whoever covers this stretch of coast.

The sections below are organised as decisions rather than as features. Who lives here and what each household's pressure point is; how to map a mid-course curriculum transfer subject by subject; whether the Diploma or A Levels fits a given student on this coast; which maths route to take and what universities publish about it; who regulates schools in each emirate; and what to do about boarding, siblings and language streams.

fujairah/al-gurfa.programmesIntro: Which programme suits a student on this coast depends less on prestige than on portability, cohort size and what the family expects to be doing in three years. All four routes below are available to Al Gurfa families, though not all within the emirate.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten externally examined subjects at the end of Year 11. Cambridge uses four-digit syllabus codes and tiers several subjects into Core and Extended; Pearson Edexcel uses its own code series with different tiering and practical assessment arrangements. The qualification is recognised internationally, which is what makes it the default choice for mobile households.
programmes.countryNote: For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track an Al Gurfa student needs five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among those five. A settled household planning on a UAE university should know that before Year 9 options are chosen, because it constrains the subject mix rather than the grades.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across Higher and Standard Level with a core of Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Broad by design, demanding in coursework, and widely recognised. The breadth suits a student who has not narrowed their interests; the coursework load punishes a student who struggles to work without supervision.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma provision on the Fujairah coast is limited, so an Al Gurfa family choosing this route is often choosing a school outside the emirate or a long commute. Cohorts where it is available are small, which means fewer subject options and fewer peers taking the same Higher Level, so the decision should be made on the actual subject list offered rather than on the programme name.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth with external examinations and no central core. The modular structure differs between Cambridge and Pearson, which changes when a result can be banked. Specialisation suits a student who already knows their direction and reduces the coursework management load considerably compared with the Diploma.
programmes.countryNote: This is the more commonly available post-16 route in British-curriculum schools on this coast. For equivalency, the British track requires one accredited subject at Advanced Level at a grade of no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, in addition to the five IGCSE subjects. Confirm the current rule on the Ministry's own pages.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each and reported as criterion levels. The programme is a strong preparation for the Diploma and a less direct preparation for IGCSE, because criterion assessment and terminal examination reward different habits. Students moving from the Middle Years Programme into IGCSE often need explicit exam-technique work.
programmes.countryNote: Families arriving in Fujairah from a Middle Years school elsewhere in the UAE sometimes find the local option is IGCSE rather than a continuation. That is a transition rather than a setback, but it needs mapping: the content overlap is high and the assessment style is not, so the work is about examination format rather than about subject knowledge.

fujairah/al-gurfa.subjectsIntro: The requests from this district split between the long-decision subjects, where a route choice matters, and the catch-up subjects a new arrival needs quickly. Both are listed, with what each actually demands.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebra, functions, trigonometry, calculus and proof, with a non-calculator paper and the Higher Level Paper 3. The route expected by most mathematics-heavy and engineering degree programmes, though every university publishes its own requirements and those should be read directly rather than assumed.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling, financial mathematics and graph theory at Higher Level, with heavy graphical calculator use. Suits students heading for social sciences, business and design courses, but some technical degrees do not accept it, so programme requirements must be checked before the route is locked in Year 11.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE 0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The gateway subject for every post-16 route. A student arriving from a different system most often needs work here first, because algebraic fluency and the expected presentation of working differ more between curricula than the content does.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Comprehension of unseen texts, grammar and extended writing in Standard Arabic, taught as a separate stream from Arabic as an additional language. Marks are lost in grammatical accuracy in extended writing, and the stream assignment a school makes in early secondary is rarely revisited even when it becomes wrong.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking for students who did not begin in Arabic. Short frequent practice beats long weekly sessions because vocabulary retention drives the grade, and students who rely on transliteration rather than reading the script fluently plateau early.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Mechanics, thermal physics, waves, electricity and fields. The subject where a curriculum transfer hurts most, because mathematical fluency and the expectation of rearranging equations under time pressure vary sharply between systems. Four to eight weeks of focused work usually closes the gap.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Stoichiometry, energetics, equilibrium, acids and bases and organic chemistry. New arrivals are often strong on recall and weak on the quantitative and practical-reasoning questions, which are precisely where the recoverable marks on a UK-style paper sit.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Cells, transport, genetics, ecology and physiology, with command terms doing heavy work. A transferring student with strong content knowledge still loses marks by answering every question with description rather than matching the response to the command term asked.

subjects.name: English A and English as a Second Language
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0500 and 0510
subjects.description: Analysis, comparative essay and oral components in the Diploma; reading, writing and sometimes speaking at IGCSE. For a student whose schooling language is changing, the first priority is register and task fulfilment in writing rather than vocabulary breadth.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0450 and 0455
subjects.description: Ownership, marketing, operations, finance and macroeconomic analysis, assessed largely through case study and data response. The dominant loss is explaining a concept without applying it to the stimulus material, which reads as competent and scores in the lower bands.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Systems, computational thinking and programming, with abstract data structures added at Higher Level. A frequent mismatch for transferring students, because prior courses vary enormously in how much actual programming they required before the examined course begins.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0460 and 0470
subjects.description: Case-study deployment, source evaluation and essay argument. Transferring students usually have content and lack structure, so essay and source planning work produces faster gains than reading more material does.

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Gurfa and what each household's pressure point is
paragraphs: The useful way to start is to identify which household you are, because the right first action differs sharply between them. A long-settled family with children already in the local school system is making decisions with a four-year horizon and no urgency this month. A family that landed eight weeks ago has urgency and no horizon. Advice that does not distinguish between them wastes the time of both.

Settled households tend to ask route questions. Which post-16 programme, which maths course, which Higher Levels, whether to stay in the emirate for sixth form or look to Sharjah. Their risk is a decision taken by default: a maths route chosen because of a timetable clash, a subject dropped because a teacher left, an Arabic stream assigned in Year 7 that nobody reviewed. None of those feels like a decision at the time and all of them are.

New arrivals ask catch-up questions and usually ask them about the wrong subject. The instinct is to worry about the subject with the lowest mark, when the subject that actually needs attention first is mathematics, because the fluency gap there limits progress in physics and chemistry simultaneously. Fixed-term households add a further constraint: if the family may leave before the exams, portability of the qualification outweighs local convenience.

The table sets out the four patterns seen most often from this district with the first action each one should take. It is a sorting tool, not a description of anybody in particular, and most real households have features of two of them.

sections.heading: Arriving mid-course: mapping the transition subject by subject
paragraphs: A curriculum change mid-course is not a general setback and should not be treated as one. The content overlap between systems is usually high; the differences sit in assessment format, mathematical expectation and the conventions of how work is presented. Treating it as a general catch-up means reteaching material the student already has while leaving the actual gap untouched.

The mapping exercise is concrete. Take each subject, find the specific topics in the new syllabus the previous course did not cover, and separate them from the topics the previous course covered differently. The first list is teaching. The second list is translation, usually faster, and often the larger of the two. Then establish which assessment conventions are new: what counts as working in mathematics, how practical skills are examined, how an essay is expected to be structured.

One practical warning about the first list. A student who has never covered a topic is not behind in the ordinary sense; they have simply not been in the room when it was taught, and a motivated sixteen-year-old closes such a gap faster than anyone expects. The slow gaps are the translation ones, where a student has met the material under a different set of conventions and keeps producing answers in the wrong form. Those feel like understanding problems to everyone involved and they are habits, which take longer to shift than new content does.

Mathematics comes first in almost every case, because fluency there limits physics and chemistry at the same time, and because algebraic presentation expectations differ more between systems than the algebra itself does. Sciences follow. Humanities and languages are usually the least urgent, not because the gap is smaller but because the gap closes through ordinary classwork more readily.

sections.heading: Diploma or A Levels for a student on the east coast
paragraphs: This is the decision settled Al Gurfa households spend most time on and the one most often made on reputation rather than fit. Both routes are widely recognised. The difference is structural: the Diploma is broad with a compulsory core and heavy self-managed coursework, while A Levels are narrow, externally examined and considerably lighter on independent project management.

Fit is mostly about two things. The first is whether the student has narrowed their interests. A student certain they are heading for engineering gains little from compulsory breadth and loses time to it; a student with no settled direction benefits from keeping options open. The second is whether the student can sustain long unsupervised work. The Diploma core assumes they can, and a student who needs chasing will find the Extended Essay and internal assessments punishing rather than enriching.

On this coast there is a third factor nobody mentions in the glossy comparisons: availability. Diploma provision in Fujairah is limited, so choosing it may mean a longer commute, a school outside the emirate, or weekly boarding. A narrower cohort also means fewer subject options within the programme, so the honest comparison is between the actual subject list each available school offers, not between the two programmes in principle.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: The maths route is the single most consequential subject decision in the Diploma, because it closes doors quietly. A student who takes Applications and Interpretation and later applies for an engineering programme that expects Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level discovers the problem at application stage, by which point nothing can be done. The reverse error, taking Analysis and Approaches unnecessarily and struggling, costs grades across the whole diploma.

The two courses are genuinely different rather than harder and easier versions of each other. Analysis and Approaches emphasises algebra, calculus and proof, with a non-calculator paper and, at Higher Level, a long problem-solving paper. Applications and Interpretation emphasises statistics, modelling, financial mathematics and, at Higher Level, graph theory and matrices, with heavy graphical calculator use throughout.

The decision should be made from two pieces of evidence rather than from preference. First, the published entry requirements of the programmes and universities the family has in mind, read from the institution's own admissions pages rather than from a summary. Universities in the UAE publish their own requirements individually, and they differ by programme within the same institution, so the only reliable source is the specific programme page. Second, the student's actual performance in algebra at IGCSE, which predicts Analysis and Approaches outcomes better than general mathematical confidence does.

sections.heading: Who regulates private schools in each emirate
paragraphs: Families moving within the UAE assume the regulatory framework travels with them, and it does not. There are five bodies, the differences are substantive, and a household in Al Gurfa planning a move to Dubai or Sharjah should know which one governs the school they are considering before they compare anything else about it.

The federal position is clear. Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in that emirate. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai. The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in Sharjah, and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge does the same there. The Ministry of Education plays a supervisory role over private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

The powers differ as well as the names. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum approval sits with the emirate regulator rather than only inspection. Dubai's authority publishes annual inspection outcomes on a six-band scale and in May 2026 confirmed there would be no increase in private school fees for the 2026-27 academic year under the emirate's second economic incentives package.

One thing no regulator does is accredit tutors. A private individual tutoring in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is a separate matter from school licensing, and any provider describing itself as approved by an education regulator should be asked to show the permit number. A tutoring operation with premises and staff needs its own educational services permit, which is again a different thing.

sections.heading: Boarding, weekly boarding and distance schooling from this coast
paragraphs: When a local option block does not carry a required subject, Al Gurfa families face a choice that Dubai families rarely have to make. The options are a long daily commute, weekly boarding in Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah, a registered distance-learning school with an external exam centre, or accepting the subject combination that is locally available. Each has a real cost and none is obviously right.

A long daily commute is the option that looks cheapest and most often fails. Two hours a day of travel is ten hours a week, which is roughly the independent study time a Diploma student needs, and it is taken from exactly the same part of the week. Weekly boarding removes the travel and adds a different problem: a student managing coursework deadlines without a parent noticing when the work is not happening.

Distance schooling suits a narrow set of households, usually where a specific subject is unavailable locally and the student is already self-managing well. The practical constraints are examination entry and practical components: an external candidate needs a centre willing to administer their papers, and not every centre can offer every component. That question should be settled before enrolment rather than after.

For any of these, the tutoring implication is the same. The subjects a student is studying without a local specialist are the ones where an online specialist match matters most, and that match is not constrained by which of these schooling options a family chooses. Lessons are delivered online one to one over live video, so nothing in the plan depends on where the student sleeps on a Tuesday.

sections.heading: Two children, one tutor, and when sharing actually works
paragraphs: Households in this district frequently have two or three children at different stages, and the question of whether one arrangement can serve more than one of them comes up early, usually for cost reasons. It sometimes can, and the conditions under which it works are narrow enough to be worth stating plainly rather than discovering by trial.

Sharing works when two students are on the same syllabus, at the same tier or level, and genuinely at a similar point in it. Two Year 11 students both sitting Cambridge 0580 Extended with similar mock profiles can share a session productively, and the explanation one gives the other is a strong test of recall for both. Siblings two years apart on different courses cannot share anything useful, and an attempt to do so produces a session that teaches neither of them.

Where sharing does not work, the better economy is usually sequencing rather than combining. Support one child properly for a term, finish, and then support the other, rather than running two thin arrangements at once. That also forces a decision about which child needs it more, which is uncomfortable and almost always clarifying.

Scheduling two children into adjacent slots on the same evening is a separate and usually good idea, because it protects the remaining evenings instead of taking a piece out of each one. For a household running several school timetables, protecting whole evenings is worth more than optimising any single session.

sections.heading: Home language, the Arabic streams and what they affect
paragraphs: In a household where Arabic is spoken at home and school is conducted in English, the student is carrying two languages of instruction across one week, and the stream the school places them in for Arabic has consequences that reach further than most families realise. The decision is often made administratively on entry and then never reviewed, even when the student's position changes.

The two streams are distinct courses, not levels of the same course. Arabic as a first language assesses comprehension of unseen texts, grammar and extended writing in Standard Arabic. Arabic as an additional language assesses functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking for students who did not begin in Arabic. Schools are required to organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ.

The equivalency consequence is the one families miss. On the British track, Ministry of Education requirements count five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A student relying on Arabic as one of their five therefore does not have five countable subjects. That is a Year 9 options decision disguised as a Year 13 administrative problem.

A home language that is neither Arabic nor English adds a third layer, and the practical priority there is register and task fulfilment in English writing rather than vocabulary breadth, because that is where the marks sit on a UK-style paper. None of these decisions is irreversible, but all of them are cheaper to review in Year 9 than to discover in Year 13.

sections.heading: A decision checklist for a family new to this coast
paragraphs: For a household that arrived recently, the order of operations matters more than the quality of any individual decision. Doing these in the wrong sequence is how families end up enrolled in a school that cannot offer a subject the student needs, or entered for a series whose deadline has passed.

First, confirm what the student is actually being entered for: board, syllabus codes, tiers and series. This is a single email to the exams officer and it governs everything downstream, including which past papers are worth doing. Second, request the previous school's transcript and, for a Diploma student, written confirmation of internal assessment progress with any marked drafts, because work that cannot be evidenced may have to be restarted.

Third, map the transition subject by subject, separating topics never covered from topics covered differently, and start with mathematics. Fourth, find out the school's internal deadline calendar for the year, which is where coursework collisions become visible. Fifth, if the family may relocate again before the exams, establish now where the student will sit the papers and whether that centre can administer the practical and speaking components.

Only then is it worth deciding about tutoring, and by that point the brief is specific enough to be useful: four weeks on algebraic fluency against Cambridge 0580 Extended, or six sessions on an internal assessment evaluation section before a draft deadline in November. A specific brief gets a specialist and a finite plan. A general one gets neither.

process.title: Say which household you are
process.description: A settled family making a route decision and a family that arrived eight weeks ago need opposite first conversations. Saying which one you are in the first message saves a session, because the diagnosis, the urgency and the subject order all follow from it.

process.title: Confirm board, code, tier and series
process.description: One email to the exams officer settles what the student will actually sit. Everything downstream depends on it, including which past papers are worth the time, and for a new arrival it sometimes reveals an entry deadline nobody had mentioned.

process.title: Map the subjects before booking hours
process.description: Separate the topics never covered from the topics covered differently. The first list needs teaching and the second needs translation, which is faster. Starting with mathematics lifts physics and chemistry at the same time.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: The first session is free and diagnostic, worked against the new syllabus rather than the old one. It ends with a written summary of the real gap and a recommended number of sessions, which for a format-only transition is often three to six.

process.title: Review the route decisions deliberately
process.description: Maths route, Arabic stream, post-16 programme and Higher Level combination all get reviewed on a date rather than drifting. Each of those is a decision taken by default if nobody puts it in the diary.

whyPoints.title: Advice framed as a decision
whyPoints.description: Settled households and new arrivals get different first conversations, because a route choice with a four-year horizon and a mid-course transfer with an entry deadline next month have nothing useful in common.

whyPoints.title: Transitions mapped, not described
whyPoints.description: A curriculum change is handled subject by subject, separating content never covered from content covered differently. That is usually a shorter and cheaper piece of work than the general catch-up families expect.

whyPoints.title: Requirements read from the source
whyPoints.description: University and equivalency requirements are read from the institution's or the Ministry's own pages rather than from a summary, because they differ by programme and change between cycles. Where a figure could not be verified, this page says so.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery survives a relocation
whyPoints.description: Lessons are taught live online, one to one. For a fixed-term household that means an arrangement that continues through a move rather than ending with it, and for everyone it means the specialist is chosen on the syllabus rather than the drive.

whyPoints.description: The emirate regulators license and inspect schools; none of them accredits a tutoring provider. Individual tutors in the UAE hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, and that is the document to ask for.

whyPoints.title: Honest about local availability
whyPoints.description: Diploma provision and narrow Higher Level teaching on this coast are limited, and this page says so rather than implying a full local service. Where a specialist is not free, you get a timeline instead of a substitute.

faqs.question: We have just moved to Al Gurfa mid-year. Which subject should we fix first?
faqs.answer: Mathematics, in almost every case, even if it is not the lowest mark. Algebraic fluency and the presentation conventions expected in working differ more between curricula than the content does, and weakness there limits progress in physics and chemistry at the same time. Fixing it lifts two other subjects at once rather than one. Then map each remaining subject by separating topics the previous course never covered from topics it covered differently; the second list is usually larger and faster to close, and it is routinely mistaken for a knowledge gap.

faqs.question: How long does a move from CBSE to IGCSE usually take to settle?
faqs.answer: For a focused transition alongside normal school attendance, typically six to twelve weeks of one-to-one work, front-loaded on mathematics. The content overlap is high; what changes is the demand for application and multi-step reasoning rather than recall, and the expectation that working is presented so method marks can be awarded independently of the answer. Students often arrive strong on content and lose marks on format, which looks like a knowledge problem and is not. A diagnostic against the new syllabus in week one saves most of the guesswork.

faqs.question: Should my child take the Diploma or A Levels if we live on the east coast?
faqs.answer: Decide on fit and availability rather than reputation. The Diploma is broad with a compulsory core and heavy self-managed coursework; A Levels are narrow, externally examined and much lighter on project management. A student with a settled direction gains little from compulsory breadth; a student who needs chasing will find the Diploma core punishing. Then look at what is actually offered locally: Diploma provision on this coast is limited, so choosing it may mean a commute, a school in another emirate or weekly boarding. Compare the real subject lists, not the programme names.

faqs.question: What is the difference between IB Maths Analysis and Applications in practice?
faqs.answer: They are different courses rather than harder and easier versions of one. Analysis and Approaches emphasises algebra, calculus, functions and proof, includes a non-calculator paper, and at Higher Level adds a long problem-solving paper. Applications and Interpretation emphasises statistics, modelling, financial mathematics and, at Higher Level, graph theory and matrices, with graphical calculator use throughout. Choose using two pieces of evidence: the published entry requirement for every target degree programme, read on the institution's own page, and the student's actual IGCSE algebra performance.

faqs.question: Can the wrong maths route close off a university course later?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the main risk of the decision. Many mathematics-heavy and engineering programmes expect Analysis and Approaches, commonly at Higher Level, while some accept Applications and Interpretation, and requirements differ by programme within the same institution. Because the problem surfaces at application stage, there is no remedy by then. UAE universities publish their own requirements individually, so the only reliable source is the specific programme page for each course under consideration, read before the route is locked in Year 11 rather than afterwards.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates our school if we move from Fujairah to Sharjah?
faqs.answer: The Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education in that emirate and also approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Fujairah's private schools, by contrast, sit under the federal Ministry of Education, which supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Dubai is governed by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority and Abu Dhabi by the Department of Education and Knowledge. The powers differ, not just the names, so check which body governs a school before comparing anything else about it.

faqs.question: Is any tutoring provider approved by KHDA or the Ministry of Education?
faqs.answer: The education regulators license and inspect schools; they do not accredit tutoring providers, so a claim of regulator approval should always be questioned. What does exist is the MoHRE private tuition work permit for individual tutors, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Ask to see it. Separately, a tutoring operation with premises and staff needs its own educational services permit from the relevant authority, which is a different document covering a different activity.

faqs.question: Does weekly boarding in Sharjah make sense for a subject not offered in Fujairah?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the comparison is against a long commute rather than against staying put. Two hours of daily travel is about ten hours a week, taken from the same part of the week a Diploma student needs for independent study, so the commute often costs more than it appears to. Weekly boarding removes that and introduces a different issue: coursework deadlines managed without a parent noticing when work is not happening. Either way, the subject with no local specialist is the one where an online match matters most.

faqs.question: Can two of our children share the same tutoring sessions?
faqs.answer: Only under narrow conditions. Sharing works when two students are on the same syllabus, at the same tier or level, and genuinely at a similar point in the course; two Year 11 students both sitting Cambridge 0580 Extended with similar mock profiles can work well together, because explaining to each other tests recall. Siblings two years apart on different courses cannot share anything useful. Where sharing does not fit, sequencing one child properly for a term and then the other beats running two thin arrangements at once.

faqs.question: Does Arabic count towards the five subjects needed for MoE equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. The published requirement on the British track is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A student relying on Arabic as one of the five therefore does not have five countable subjects, which turns a Year 9 options decision into a Year 13 problem. Equivalency is administered by the Ministry of Education and no tutoring provider performs or guarantees it; confirm the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on any summary.

faqs.question: Why are Arabic classes split into first-language and additional-language streams?
faqs.answer: Because they are different courses with different curriculum expectations and different languages of instruction. First-language Arabic assesses comprehension of unseen texts, grammar and extended writing in Standard Arabic; additional-language Arabic assesses functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking. Published guidance requires schools to organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combined classes for the two groups. Support material written for one stream is the wrong material for the other, so the stream assignment should be confirmed before booking anything.

faqs.question: Our posting may end before the exams. What should we settle now?
faqs.answer: Where the papers will be sat and by which board. Confirm the syllabus codes, tiers and series in writing, then establish whether a centre at the likely destination can administer the student's components, because practical and speaking components are the usual constraint for an external or transferring candidate. Entry deadlines sit months before exams: Cambridge entries for the March 2027 series were due on 27 November 2026, for example. Settling this early is what keeps a relocation from costing a series rather than a term.

faqs.question: How do we avoid making a route decision by accident?
faqs.answer: Put each decision in the diary with a date. The maths route, the Arabic stream, the post-16 programme and the Higher Level combination are all decisions that get taken by default if nobody schedules them: a subject dropped because a teacher left, a stream assigned in Year 7 and never reviewed, a route chosen around a timetable clash. None of those feels like a choice at the time. Reviewing them explicitly in Year 9 and again in Year 11, against marked work and against published university requirements, is the whole of the fix.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring a compromise for a family living this far from Dubai?
faqs.answer: On this coast it is generally the better option rather than the fallback. Fujairah has small school cohorts, so the pool of local teachers with experience of any single Higher Level course is thin, and for narrow subjects it can be effectively empty within the emirate. Online matching removes the geographic limit and lets the specialist be chosen on the syllabus rather than on willingness to drive the coast road. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; lessons are taught live online, one to one, with the first one free.

faqs.question: What should a new arrival ask the school in the first week?
faqs.answer: Five things, in this order. Which board, syllabus codes, tiers and series the student will be entered for. Whether the previous school's transcript and any evidenced coursework progress have been received. What the internal deadline calendar for the year looks like. Which subjects the option block can actually accommodate for this student in this year group. And, for a Diploma student, which subject each Extended Essay supervisor specialises in. The answers determine what kind of support is needed, which is a cheaper question than how much.

A settled household weighing a maths route for Year 12 needs a different first session from a family that arrived last month with a Year 10 student mid-transfer. What is worth reading in a profile is narrow: the subjects at the exact level, the syllabus history, and whether they will mark a script against the published criteria in front of you.

intro.heading: A question with no published answer, and what to ask instead
paragraphs: There is no register of tutor quality in the UAE, no inspection band for a tutoring provider, and no authority that ranks them. So when a page announces that it has the finest IB tutors on the east coast, the claim is not merely unverified; there is nothing it could be verified against. The research behind this site found competitor pages publishing a 4.92 rating from 480 reviews and a 4.93 from 850 on the same page, and another showing a perfect score from twenty reviews next to a claim of 2,500 students taught. Those are not evidence. They are decoration.

What does exist is a set of checkable facts. Whether the person teaching holds the MoHRE private tuition work permit. Whether they have taught the exact syllabus at the exact level. Whether they will mark your child's script against the published assessment criteria while you watch. What the market charges, with the source named. What happens if the match is wrong after two sessions. None of those require trust, and a provider who answers all five in writing has told you more than any rating could.

Timing is the other half of the question, because the best available tutor at the wrong point in the calendar is a poor purchase. A family in the first term of DP1 should be buying foundations and internal assessment design. A family eight weeks from the papers should be buying marked scripts and topic triage. A family in MYP 4 should be buying a criterion diagnosis. The same tutor, the same hourly rate, three different jobs - and a provider who does not ask the date before quoting has not started working yet.

This page is therefore organised as a verification checklist and a timeline rather than as a pitch. It sets out what to ask and what a non-answer tells you, what should be visibly different after four weeks and after a term, what the AED bands actually signal, and which claims are a reason to stop the conversation. Some of what follows argues against buying anything at all, which is the honest consequence of writing a checklist rather than an advertisement.

IB Gram works with Fujairah families online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time, starting with a free trial lesson. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE - home visits are a service we run only in India - and we hold no accreditation from KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, because no such accreditation exists for a tutoring platform. What we publish instead is the market rate, the delivery format, the boundaries on coursework, and what happens when no specialist is free.

fujairah/best-ib-tutor.programmesIntro: What counts as a good tutor changes with the programme, because the thing being assessed changes. These are the three stages east-coast families hire for, with the specific competence to look for in each.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led with no criterion marking, so there is nothing to drill and no paper to practise. A good tutor at this stage is building reading fluency, number confidence and the habit of producing a structured written answer. The warning sign is a tutor who introduces worksheets and tests; the useful signal is one who can say what a six-year-old should be able to do by the end of a term.
programmes.countryNote: Few Fujairah schools run a full Primary Years Programme, so local primary classes mix several curricula. Any plan should start from what the child's own school is teaching rather than from a generic year-group expectation.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject marked out of eight. The competence to test for is whether a tutor can name the criteria in the subject group they are being hired for, and say which one your child is losing marks on from the marked work in front of them. A tutor who opens an MYP session with a past paper has misread the programme, because in MYP 1 to 3 no external paper exists.
programmes.countryNote: In small Fujairah cohorts the same teacher often covers several MYP years, so a persistent criterion weakness can go unnamed for a long time. That makes the diagnosis itself the thing worth paying for first.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three normally at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. The test here is level-specific: has this tutor taught the subject at Higher Level, and will they mark a timed answer against the published criteria now. Internal assessment work raises an honesty question too, and a straight answer about what they will and will not do with a draft is part of the assessment.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma provision on this coast is thin, so the subject a family most needs is often the one with no local specialist. For those requests the honest sequence is availability first, then price, then personality - not the reverse.

programmes.name: Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS
programmes.description: Supervised by the school, and the place where outside help is most easily misused. A competent tutor will ask what the school supervisor has already said, will teach the criteria, and will decline to supply text. One who offers to deliver a finished essay is not a better tutor; they are a risk to the candidate, since the work submitted must be the student's own.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Fujairah school has one staff member supervising several essays across unfamiliar subjects, outside support is genuinely valuable. It should still sit behind the supervisor rather than in competition with them.

fujairah/best-ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: A profile that lists twenty subjects tells you nothing. These are the subjects Fujairah families hire for most, each with the one question that separates a specialist from a generalist.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Ask which Higher Level paper they find students struggle with most and why. A specialist will talk about extended problem-solving and proof rather than about algebra in general. Ask also how they would structure the exploration without touching the student's own writing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Ask how they teach graphic display calculator use for the modelling questions. The route is technology-centred, and a tutor trained only on Analysis and Approaches will undervalue exactly the skills this course assesses.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Ask how they mark a multi-step calculation that reaches the right answer with missing working. The answer reveals whether they teach to the mark scheme or to the subject. Ask separately what they will do with an internal investigation draft.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Ask which command terms students answer wrongly and what the difference between describe and explain costs in marks. A specialist answers in examples; a generalist answers in generalities about understanding concepts.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Ask how they handle data-based questions, since that is where prepared students separate from well-read ones. Also ask how they would narrow an over-ambitious investigation question without designing it for the student.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Ask what a diagram is worth in a long answer and how they teach evaluation. Then ask how they would help with the commentaries without selecting the articles or writing the analysis, which is the real boundary question in this subject.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Ask how they teach application marks from stimulus material. Students from family-business households often write knowledgeably and answer the wrong question, and a tutor who recognises that pattern immediately is worth more than one with a longer subject list.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Ask them to analyse an unseen short extract in front of you. Five minutes of that is more informative than any amount of discussion about essay structure, and it is the fastest test available in any subject on this list.

subjects.name: English B and second languages
subjects.description: Ask which text types the course requires and how they teach register. Many east-coast students sit a second language alongside Arabic, so ask how they would sequence work when two language courses peak in the same weeks.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Ask what share of the marks sits in the written papers rather than in the solution. A tutor who talks only about code has misjudged the assessment, and this is one of the subjects most often thinly staffed in a small school.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Ask how an example earns marks in a knowledge argument. The essay is marked on the quality of argument about knowledge rather than on subject content, which is why strong subject teachers are not automatically good at teaching it.

fujairah/best-ib-tutor.regionsIntro: What families ask for first differs across the emirate, mostly because of which schools and which subjects are involved. These notes describe the requests rather than the scenery.

regions.name: Fujairah City
regions.note: Most enquiries from here start with a single Diploma subject the school covers at Standard Level and the student wants at Higher Level. The verification question that matters is whether the tutor has taught the Higher Level course, not merely the subject.

regions.name: Al Faseel
regions.note: Requests cluster around MYP 4 and 5 reports, where a criterion has been low for several terms. The useful first purchase is a diagnosis rather than a package, and the trial session is usually enough to produce one.

regions.name: Sakamkam
regions.note: Later transport means an early evening slot rarely holds, so families here should be sceptical of any provider who will not commit to a 6pm start for the whole year. Consistency is a quality signal in itself.

regions.name: Merashid
regions.note: Students attend several different schools, so sibling requests often involve two curricula at once. Ask whether each child gets a subject specialist or whether one tutor is being stretched across both; the answer tells you how the provider actually matches.

regions.name: Al Gurfa
regions.note: Long school journeys make the in-home option particularly unattractive here once travel is priced, and published in-home bands reach AED 500 an hour. Enquiries from this stretch of coast are usually about reliability before they are about price.

regions.name: Dibba Al-Fujairah
regions.note: Families at the northern end sometimes use schools across the Sharjah boundary, which changes the regulator and the term calendar. A tutor who asks which school before quoting is doing the right thing.

regions.name: Qidfa and Mirbah
regions.note: The smallest communities generate the narrowest requests: one unusual Higher Level subject, no local specialist. Here the first honest answer is about availability, and a provider who promises a match without checking is telling you something.

schoolClusters.city: Fujairah schools families are hiring around
schoolClusters.note: Private schools in the emirate are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education. A tutor worth hiring will ask which school, because internal deadlines, option blocks and assessment calendars differ between them even within one district.
schools: Our Own English High School, Fujairah

schoolClusters.city: Schools outside the emirate in the same conversation
schoolClusters.note: East-coast families comparing provision often have a second school in view, in Sharjah, Ras Al Khaimah or Dubai, each under a different regulator. A provider should be able to work with either calendar rather than assuming a Dubai term structure.

fujairah/best-ib-tutor.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named only as context for the programmes available to families on this coast; no affiliation, endorsement or partnership with any school or group is implied.
fujairah/best-ib-tutor.modesIntro: Three ways of starting, all live online and one-to-one on Gulf Standard Time. The first one is free and is the only one worth buying before the others are considered.

modes.title: The trial, treated as an audition
modes.description: One free lesson in which the tutor teaches rather than sells. Give them a marked piece of work beforehand and listen for whether they name a specific weakness by the end. A session that produces only encouragement and a recommendation to book a package has failed the audition, whatever it cost.

Most of the hour should be teaching, not conversation
Ends with a named weakness and a number of weeks
No card details required, one per student

modes.title: A four-week trial block
modes.description: Where the trial goes well, four weekly sessions is long enough to see whether anything changes and short enough that a wrong decision costs little. It also lets a family test the thing that actually matters over two years: whether the slot holds and the notes arrive.
bullets: Four sessions, same tutor, same subject
A written note after each one
Reviewed against a fresh marked piece at the end
Rematch without a new fee if it is not working

modes.title: Term-long subject support
modes.description: Only after the first two. A full term follows the school's own assessment calendar, with checkpoints on marked work agreed in advance rather than reviewed by feel. For a Diploma Higher Level subject this is the shape that matters, because continuity across two years outperforms any individual session.

sections.heading: What best can honestly mean when nobody publishes evidence
paragraphs: No UAE authority inspects, rates or ranks private tutoring providers. KHDA inspects Dubai private schools and issues permits to training institutes with premises; ADEK does the equivalent in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain; the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge regulate their emirates; and the federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. None of them produces a league table of tutors. A provider claiming a regulator's endorsement is therefore describing something that does not exist.

That vacuum gets filled with self-generated proof. The competitor research behind this site found a page showing two different star ratings with two different review counts, another asserting a perfect score from twenty reviews while claiming a four-figure student total, and schema markup carrying ratings that contradicted the visible page. Google's own structured-data policy treats self-serving review markup as a violation, and in a UAE commercial context an unsupportable claim about a service is a consumer-protection exposure as well as a credibility problem.

So the sensible move is to stop looking for the best tutor and start looking for a verifiable match. Verifiable means the permit exists, the subject and level history is specific, the marking is demonstrated rather than described, the price is stated with its basis, and the exit terms are written down. A provider who meets that standard may or may not employ the finest teacher on the coast, but you will know what you are buying, which is more than any ranking offers.

sections.heading: The eight claims you can actually verify before paying
paragraphs: Each row in the table below is a claim tutoring providers make, with the way it is usually presented and the way to test it. None of the tests takes more than a message or two, and the pattern of answers is more informative than any single reply. A provider who answers six out of eight precisely and goes vague on the other two has told you exactly where the weakness is.

Two of the rows deserve emphasis. The permit question is factual: the private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years, so there is no cost reason for a legitimate tutor to be evasive. And the examiner question is one to approach carefully, because examiner status is widely claimed, rarely evidenced, and should never be presented as access to marking, boundaries or paper content.

The last row is the one families skip. Ask what happens when no suitable tutor is available for a narrow subject at a workable hour. Every provider has a coverage limit; the research found that none of the ranking competitors discloses one, and several route UAE parents to numbers in other countries without saying where the teaching happens. An honest answer to that question is worth more than a confident answer to the other seven. Run the whole list by message rather than by phone, for two reasons. A written reply can be compared against what happens later, and a provider who will put the permit, the level history and the exit terms in writing has already accepted that you may hold them to it. Anyone who insists on a call before answering any of the eight is managing the conversation rather than answering it.
